## TOP FINDS ACROSS ALL SESSIONS (16, with verdicts)

1. **@RyNoonan's audited tackle-prop record** (Session 3, tranche 2) — 939-742, +95.5 units since 2022 at ≥5% edge, self-published with a published self-correction; recorded as **the strongest provenance class in the tranche**. Attributed track record, not independently audited by Motif.
2. **@refereeinsider integrity findings** (Session 3, tranche 2) — his stated Week 5 record (33-25) does not match his own weeklies (34-25); a crew bias flipped after a follower's correction; chart lines changed in recaps and scored as wins. **DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY stands — the findings are why.** The rigorous replacement (crew assignment + penalty mix measured in-house) is C-297.
3. **@KoalatyStats defensive target funnels — 4 of 5 REPRODUCED, 1 FAILED** (Session 7, recomputed from nflverse Weeks 1–7): GB 2nd-highest WR target share allowed ✓ · DET 3rd-most pass attempts allowed ✓ · DET 2nd-highest TE target share allowed ✓ · SF/ATL funnel to RBs ✓ · **DET highest PROE allowed ✗ NOT REPRODUCED** (DET ranks 7th–11th across six definitions; Miami #1 under every season-long variant).
4. **Missed-tackle endpoints (@sfdata9ers vs PFR)** (Session 7) — DET fewest missed tackles **REPRODUCED** (12; next team 18); top-3 and bottom-3 clusters **CLOSE** (same teams, order swaps inside each cluster). PFR's MTkl table is free and programmatically reachable — GSE can own this table.
5. **Catchable Ball Rate is NOT computable from public data** (Session 7) — it is SIS/ESPN human charting (CTBL%). The one dataset class the engine cannot synthesize from play-by-play.
6. **Altitude — @mockingboardapp's created metric** (Session 4) — methodology verified from the product's own glossary: de-noised EPA/dropback for QBs, "earned yards" for skill players, split-half ingredient selection, published single-game reliability (QB 0.147, TE 0.449, WR 0.356, RB 0.307). A design reference for honest metric-building: "delete provable luck, never add identity."
7. **Fantasy Points Data Suite 2.0** (Sessions 2 + 4) — the premier external charted-data validation set (coverage shells, separation, pressure; 225K+ charted plays). **Constraint: its ToS bars scraping and commercial use without written consent** — internal validation and attributed content only. Price UNVERIFIED (behind subscribe flow).
8. **Box Score Scout's xFP** (Session 3) — per-opportunity expected fantasy points, trained 2009–2025 then FROZEN, deliberately excluding QB quality/OL/lines/weather; the author's own stated limit is on the record ("not a better forecast of future points than the points themselves"). Free, no account. Not to be conflated with PFF's different xFP (C-305).
9. **@Dan1ro0's Polymarket "Bayesian Quant" claims — verdict: UNVERIFIED marketing, do not allocate** (Session 2) — self-reported PnL, no verification path, and Polymarket's Jan–Mar 2026 dynamic-fee/delay changes structurally punish the exact taker strategy on the exact markets named.
10. **@the_waldman's +23.8 units — still UNVERIFIED** (Session 7) — no public methodology or auditable record was found; the claim stands labeled, not believed.
11. **SumerSports' ~55% equilibrium methodology — NOT FINDABLE** (Session 7) — the pass-rate equilibrium figure (~55% vs NFL's actual ~54%) is usable as a prior; the published methodology behind SumerSports' version could not be located, so it stays UNVERIFIED as a source claim.
12. **Petersen & Zech, "Mathematical theory of deep learning" (arXiv:2407.18384)** (Session 7) — verified at source; **ADOPT** into the arXiv program as a theory reference.
13. **PocketContext pressure-vs-blitz gap decomposition** (Session 8, EXTRA100 A1) — pressure rate minus blitz rate faced, split by QB: the gap separates what a protection scheme allows from what a QB invites. Reproducible from NGS pressure/blitz splits GSE already pulls. **LEARN-ONLY**; register S113.
14. **NGS provenance reconciliation — GB 47%** (Session 8, EXTRA100 §C) — Green Bay pressured Bryce Young on 47% of dropbacks in the CAR game per NGS (@NextGenStats via @MinaKimes); the circulating 52% figure was the prior week's Tampa game, and SumerSports charting separately says 52.2% for the CAR game. Three numbers, three provenances, now kept separate.
15. **Hermes Tuning Masterclass repo** (Session 8, EXTRA100 F1) — jasonjeske/hermes-master-class, 7★, license NOASSERTION, **VERIFIED** at the repo this run: version-pinned Hermes tuning doctrine (Vol. 6 measured on v0.22.5) plus a `skills/hermes-tune` weekly audit skill, aimed at an agent Garrett actually runs. **TEST**; register S114.
16. **Defensive Stuff Rate top-10, values in text** (Session 8, EXTRA100 A2) — share of opponent rush attempts stopped at or behind the line: Bengals 23.1% (#1), Steelers 21.7, Browns 21.1, Bills 20.8, Seahawks 20.6, Packers 20.0, Ravens 19.8, Buccaneers 19.4, Vikings 19.3, Falcons 18.7 (@PattonAnalytics via @StatRankings). Rare for the x_search route: the full table is text-carried. **LEARN-ONLY**.

The standing lane: `gse-analytics-sweep-am` (~09:08 CT) + `gse-analytics-sweep-pm` (~21:08 CT) from Sep 18, plus the broader `gse-x-intel-sweep` every 8 hours from Oct 6 — up to 5 runs a day over a standing 21-account list plus the @GalaxySportsHQ home feed and keyword searches (EPA / CPOE / TPRR / pass rush win rate / aggressiveness). Below are that compilation's complete front matter (what it is, schedule history, CSV census, full 83-run index) and its complete gap audit, followed by the lane's distilled product in full: the cited knowledge base (1,476 entries), which restates everything the lane learned as cited, deduped entries — who said it, when, what it is, and how the engine uses it. # NFL Advanced-Analytics Sweep — EVERY REPORT (2026-09-17 → 2026-10-16)

Compiled 2026-10-16 for Garrett. This is the complete run history of the twice-daily NFL
advanced-analytics X sweep lane: every report the lane produced, in chronological order,
reproduced in full from the repo of record, with a gap audit at the end naming every window
that produced no report and every artifact that could not be matched.

## What this is

- **83 runs compiled** — the 2026-09-17 founding manual sweep, the 2026-09-18 research pass
  the lane was patterned on, every scheduled run that produced a report through the
  2026-10-16 21:08 evening run, and one attempted run that was blocked and produced
  nothing (Run 34, kept as its own entry so the hole is visible).
- **98 AGENTS.md sections reproduced verbatim** (89 sweep sections + the founding day's 9
  per-find benchmark sections), each quoted in full under its run — metrics, definitions,
  sample values, stated data sources, caveats, and the runs' own gap flags.
- **804 new-metric / composite entries** as marked in the reports themselves (counted from
  each report's NEW-items list, its (NEW …) tags, or its numbered inventory items — the
  counting basis is printed in every run entry).
- **764 full-table CSV filenames named across the reports.** On the repo today
  (Beexly/Sports@main) there are **942 CSVs under `docs/**/full-tables/` plus 10
  chart-read CSVs** — the per-date census is in the table below. (Early reports cite
  `docs/research/<date>/…` paths; the files were reorganized under `docs/dfs/research/…`
  in the 2026-09-18 lock-in push, so a report's cited path and today's path can differ.)
- Sources cross-checked: Beexly/Sports `AGENTS.md` on remote main (blob
  `e18f9b4f5e5a7c4bbfa84c5e8f435c717640e0b0`, 1,855,725 bytes — the spine), 79 run-log /
  staged-report files in the goal's `hidden_files/`, 39 `x-intel-*.md` broad-lane files,
  the repo tree census of `full-tables/`, and the daily memory logs 2026-09-17 → 2026-10-16.

## §1a — The compilation's own gap audit (full)

# GAP AUDIT

Completeness is the point of this document, so the holes are listed with the same care as
the reports. Counts are given for every category.

## A. Scheduled windows with NO report (10) + 1 blocked attempt

Expected windows: 90 (daily lane 09:08 + 21:08 CT, 2026-09-18 → 2026-10-16 = 58; broad
lane 00:20 / 08:20 / 16:20 CT from its 2026-10-06 08:20 CT start = 32). Reports exist for
79 windows. The 11 windows without a report:

1. **2026-09-23 AM** (daily) — no section, no run log, no CSVs attributable. Nothing in the
   record shows the run was attempted. The PM run that day (Run 14) covered a ~24h window.
2. **2026-10-02 AM** (daily) — the cron FAILED before starting: runtime model-resolution
   timeouts hit several morning jobs that day (memory log 2026-10-02, which lists
   gse-analytics-sweep-am among the missed and logged as an owed retry; the retry never
   happened). No section, no run log.
3. **2026-10-03 PM** (daily) — never ran; left no run log (memory log 2026-10-04 says so
   explicitly). Its window was absorbed by the 2026-10-04 AM run (Run 33, ~24h window).
4. **2026-10-04 PM** (daily) — no run, no section, no log. Its window was absorbed by the
   2026-10-05 PM run (Run 35), which covered ~48h (2026-10-04 AM → 2026-10-05 PM).
5. **2026-10-05 AM** (daily) — ATTEMPTED AND BLOCKED (Run 34): both browser tasks failed
   (browser VM lease unavailable / circuit breaker open); X was never reached. Run log
   exists; zero findings, zero CSVs, no AGENTS.md section. Counted separately from the 10
   no-run windows because the attempt is documented.
6. **2026-10-06 09:08** (daily) — no separate run. The broad job's first run (08:22 CT)
   covered the overnight window ending 08:35 CT and its report is Run 36; the 09:08 job
   left no log or section of its own that day.
7. **2026-10-06 16:20** (broad) — no run, no report. (That day's runs: 08:22 broad and the
   evening daily run.)
8. **2026-10-07 08:20** (broad) — no run. (That day's runs: 00:20, 09:08, 16:20, 21:08.)
9. **2026-10-08 00:20** (broad) — no run. (That day's runs: 08:20, 09:08, 16:20, 21:08.)
10. **2026-10-09 08:20** (broad) — no run. (That day's runs: 00:20, 09:08, 16:20, 21:08.)
11. **2026-10-11 00:20** (broad) — no run. (That day's runs: 08:20, 09:08, 16:20, 21:08.)

## C. Coverage gaps the runs themselves recorded (aggregated)

The reports are unusually honest about their own blind spots; the standing ones, counted
across the 89 sweep sections in AGENTS.md:

- **@FTNData protected** (no follow requested, read-only rule) — flagged in **79** sections.
- **@NerdingonNFL timeline would not render** — flagged in **72** sections.
- **@NFLResearcher timeline would not render** — flagged in **66** sections.
- **Keyword-search boundary not reached** (the EPA firehose is the usual case) — **10**
  sections state a search boundary was NOT reached, meaning their search finds are a
  covered slice, not a zero.
- Truncated post tails, logo-only team identifications, and per-chart transcription
  caveats recur throughout and are preserved inside each report as written.
- Two named loose ends from the runs: **@AjayTakes “Robbed Score”** was reported missing
  for 4–6 straight sweeps, then **RESOLVED in the 2026-10-05 PM report** (Run 35) — the
  metric was confirmed and inventoried. The **“Bryce Young map”** screenshot from the

  report (Run 40, which records a Latest-search check finding no new appearance) and is

## §1b — The cited knowledge base (full text)

Built Oct 16 from the compilation: **1,476 entries after dedupe — 870 Metrics · 396 Findings · 127 Data endpoints · 83 Innovation candidates — from 222 distinct accounts**, ordered by first sighting, run by run. 329 entries carry a "posted before <run>" fallback because the source reports never recorded the post's own timestamp; 62 entries are unattributed in their reports. This knowledge base is the sweep lane's master index as well as its findings record.

# Analytics Sweep — CITED KNOWLEDGE BASE (2026-09-17 → 2026-10-16)

Built 2026-10-16 for Garrett, from the sweep-lane compilation
(`analytics-sweep-all-reports-2026-10-16.md`: all 83 runs, the 98 AGENTS.md sections
verbatim, the run-log digests, and the gap audit). This document restates everything the
lane learned as individual cited entries: who said it, when they posted it, when the sweep
found it, what it is, the context it appeared in, and how the engine uses it.

## How to read an entry

- **Said by** — the account (and person/org name where the report gives one) that posted
  the item. Items the reports never attributed say so; site-level sources are headed
  `— source` instead of an account.
- **Posted** — the source post's own date/time, exactly as the sweep report recorded it.
  Where a report never recorded the post's own timestamp, the entry reads
  "posted before <run date + label> sweep" — no post date was invented anywhere in this
  document. **329 of 1,476 entries** use that fallback, and **62 entries** are
  unattributed in their reports (mostly data-endpoint/site entries).
- **Found** — the sweep run (number + date + run label) that inventoried the item.
- **What it is** — the definition and numbers as reported, verbatim. Values the reports
  flagged as approximate, truncated, illegible, unverified, or withdrawn are flagged the
  same way here.
- **Context** — what the post/chart was doing (leaderboard, full table, model output,
  methodology explainer, thread, search find…).
- **How the engine uses it** — the application the reports themselves note (ingestion
  source, benchmark, method to adopt, signal candidate at weight 0 until evidence). Where
  no report ever assessed an application, the entry says
  "cataloged; application not yet assessed" — nothing was fabricated.

## Counts

- **1,476 entries** after dedupe: **870 Metrics · 396 Findings · 127 Data endpoints ·
  83 Innovation candidates**
- **222 distinct accounts** appear as entry sources.
- **82 of 83 runs** produced entries (Run 34, the 2026-10-05 AM attempt, was blocked and
  produced nothing — see the gap note at the end).
- **Dedupe:** the compilation's reports marked ~804 new-metric/composite items; this
  knowledge base is larger because bundled report items were split into their distinct
  sub-metrics, data endpoints and innovation candidates were given their own entries, and
  inventoried finds in the early unmarked runs were included. Where the same metric from
  the same account recurred as a running feature, the first sighting carries the full
  entry and later sightings are one-line **Update** lines under it — **151 Update lines**
  in total (114 applied inside run ranges during the build, 37 more folded across run
  ranges at merge, each fold condensing the later report's values to its headline
  numbers; the full values remain in the compilation).

Entries are ordered by first sighting — run by run, 2026-09-17 → 2026-10-16.

- Posted: Sep 17 2026
- Found: Run 1 · 2026-09-17 founding manual sweep
- What it is: Week 1 pass attempts split by progression read (primary vs secondary reads). Quantifies how often a QB works past his first read — Kyle's note: Caleb Williams "did in fact have secondary read pass attempts in Week 1." Track the scramble-counting convention before comparing vendors. Engine gap: no read-progression charting (nflverse and the FTN-via-nflverse subset do not carry read number).

- Update — Run 1, 2026-09-17: @DonAtkinsonNFL quote-post details: Columns: First Read %, Second Read %, Designated Receiver* %, Checkdown %, Scramble %. ### StatRankings JS / Odds-Engine Formulas — source
- Type: Finding
- Said by: not attributed in the report (JS codebase intel, 2026-09-18, full 102-file mine)
- Posted: posted before 2026-09-18 research pass
- Found: Run 2 · 2026-09-18 research pass
- What it is: Formulas: implied probability = price>0 ? 100/(price+100) : -price/(-price+100), rounded to 0.1%. Survivor favored = winPct >= 58; FAV LEFT = remaining favored non-bye weeks; bands >=75/>=60/>=50. Admin projection review: >10% off baseline tints cell (DISCREPANCY_THRESHOLD), >20% off market line = edge flag. Coverage shells: Man = 0,1,2M; Zone = 2,3,4,6,9 (order 0,1,2,2M,3,4,6,9). Free/gated boundaries: free presets = All Games, Last 1, Last 3 only; Last 5/10, Home/Away, specific weeks, Custom Split column gated. Infra: AWS Cognito auth, CloudFront CDN, Stripe hosted checkout, Rewardful referrals, Google One Tap, GA4. No secrets/keys in client code.

### HB Analytics Run Block Grade (Disruption Rate Grade) — @hawkblogger
- Type: Innovation candidate
- Said by: @hawkblogger
- Posted: 2026-09-25 5:58 PM CDT
- Found: Run 18 · 2026-09-25 PM
- What it is: "Top 20 Run Blocking OL (T, G, C) Through Week 2". Metric: "Run block grade" = "Disruption rate grade". Author methodology (verbatim): "Sumer Sports charts every run play by player: which blockers each defender faced, on every snap. A blocker's grade is how much he moves the disruption rate on a typical rep, compared with an average blocker facing the same defenders. Lower is better, so the best grades are negative. Bars always point right for a good grade. Every rep counts who was across from him. Winning against a top defender counts for more than winning against a backup, and every defender's own grade is worked out at the same time. Double teams are handled on their own, so a player who draws extra blockers is not marked down for it. Players with few reps are pulled toward average until the sample earns a strong grade. Games used: Blended = 2026 through Week 3, with 2025 counted at 50% and fading out by Week 6. Trend compares this season with his own past: his reps this year against what his earlier grade predicted against the same opponents. Over expected is the running total: disruptions above or below what an average blocker would have had against the same opponents." Top 5 of 20 (rank, player, pos-team, grade, trend, reps, disruptions, over expected): 1. Garett Bolles, OT-DEN, -2.6, -1.1, 560, 29, -17.5 | 2. Penei Sewell, OT-DET, -2.6, -2.8, 480, 30, -10.6 | 3. Filters OT/G/C, 150+ reps, played in 2026. FLAG: post title says "Through Week 2" but chart says "through Week 3". Data: "Sumer Sports play-by-player charting · stats.hawkblogger.com"; brand "HB ANALYTICS".
- Context: Top-20 leaderboard; report calls the HB Analytics family the strongest innovation kernel of the day — opponent-adjusted, double-team-aware, Bayesian-shrunk, time-blended grades.

Overton (DAL) +1.1/-- 46/6 +1.7; 16 Ashton Gillotte (KC) +1.0/+1.3 48/6 +1.6; 17 Donovan Ezeiruaku (DAL) +0.9/+1.4 95/11 +2.3; 18 Nick Herbig (PIT) +0.8/+1.1 49/5 +1.1; 19 Jalyx Hunt (PHI) +0.6/+1.7 82/9 +1.4; 20 YaYa Diaby (TB) +0.6/+0.8 56/6 +0.9. Columns: PLAYER | GRADE | TREND | REPS | DISRUPTIONS | OVER EXP. Author's method (chart's "How the grade works," summarized in report): each defender's run-stopping graded on every snap; grade = how much he moves disruption rate on a typical rep vs an average defender facing the same blockers (higher better); wins vs top blockers count more; double teams handled; low-rep players pulled toward average until a strong grade; TREND compares season vs past; "Over Expected" = disruptions above/below an average defender against the same opponents. Stated source: Sumer Sports player-by-player charting; stats.hawkblogger.com. Caveats: 2026 games only, EDGE, 1+ reps; low-rep players pulled toward average. Attributed inconsistency: chart header says "this season's games through Week 5"; post text says "through 4 weeks."
- Context: New leaderboard with methodology explainer.
- How the engine uses it: Marginal run-disruption grade vs average defender on identical blocking matchups, with an Over-Expected vs-same-opponents term (report's innovation kernel).

## Part 1 — Bookmarks

### B1–B3 · The @FantasyPtsData Week 1 cluster (3 bookmarks, one dossier)

**The items:**
- **B1** (Sep 14) — RB leaders in RYOE/attempt, Week 1: Monangai +5.69 at the top, Barkley +0.77 at the bottom of the shown list. Image post. https://x.com/FantasyPtsData/status/2099580357133660429
- **B2** (Sep 14) — Jahmyr Gibbs hit 50+ snaps, 25+ carries, 5+ targets in Week 1 — a workload line reached only 30 times in FantasyPtsData history, averaging 28.1 fantasy points per game.
- **B3** (Sep 15) — De'Von Achane: 88% snap share, 14.8% target share; 98 historical instances of that usage profile, averaging 20.3 FPG.

**What these are:** output from Fantasy Points' charted-data operation (see B4). RYOE = Rushing Yards Over Expected per attempt: actual rushing yards minus what a model expects an average back to gain given field position, defensive alignment, and situation. The Gibbs and Achane posts are *usage-rarity* posts — they take one game's snap/carry/target line, count how often history has produced it, and report what those players averaged.

**Why he saved them (lane fit — GSE):** these are signal-mining bookmarks, not trivia. All three are Week 1 inputs for exactly the questions the GSE engine answers in September: whose workload is real, whose efficiency is noise. The Gibbs/Achane pattern (workload rarity → historical scoring average) is a base-rate lookup he can run against any Week 1 breakout.

**Cost & effectiveness (evidence-based, and this is the honest part):** the two halves of this cluster have very different evidentiary value.
- *Usage signals (B2, B3) — durable.* Snap share and opportunity share are among the most stable week-to-week fantasy stats; a documented historical base rate (30 instances → 28.1 FPG; 98 instances → 20.3 FPG) is a legitimate prior.
- *RYOE (B1) — weak at this sample.* Independent analysis of over-expected metrics (nFelo) finds RYOE has almost no year-to-year predictiveness — a rusher's RYOE sign is close to a coin flip season to season, and it takes roughly four seasons of data before RYOE carries the signal of simpler metrics. One *week* of RYOE/attempt (Monangai +5.69) is noise-grade: useful as a "watch this back" flag, worthless as a projection input on its own.

**How to use it:** treat B1 as a watch-list trigger only; treat B2/B3's method — workload line → historical instance count → average outcome — as the reusable template. It is the same shape as his own engine's situational base rates.

**Launch steps:** none required (bookmarks already serve their purpose as reference). If he wants this systematically: the Data Suite (B4) is the tool that generates these tables on demand.

### B4 · Fantasy Points Data Suite 2.0 — the product behind the bookmarks

**The item:** @FantasyPtsData, Sep 8 — "Data Suite 2.0 is here!" launch post (video), linking fantasypointsdata.com.

**What it is:** a subscription web app of charted NFL data — not scraped box scores. Fantasy Points' own team (20+ charters, process built by Brett Whitefield, ex-PFF/FTN) hand-charts every play across eight charting processes: coverage shells (Cover 0–6, man/zone, one-high/two-high, disguised looks), route detail (alignment, break type/depth, separation grade — including on routes never targeted), pressure/protection (blitz, stunt, box count, time to throw/pressure), run concepts (zone/gap, gap attacked, yards before/after contact), and participation (snaps, route participation, honest denominators). 40+ research tools, 2,000+ stat columns, 225K+ charted plays, six chart types, player/team/coach profiles, saved views, CSV export of any table.

**What's new in 2.0 (from the vendor's own changelog):** team offense/defense tables with coaching splits (head coach, OC, playcaller, DC — usable across mid-season staff changes), a Starting QB split, a "Likely Pass Situation" play filter (≥70% predicted pass), drive-level filtering, EPA/Play that counts designed QB runs, an explosive-play rate column for receiving, and continued weekly feature drops through the 2026 season (defense-vs-position validated to 99.7% against their CSV, coverage matrices, percentile display mode, smarter CSV export). This is an actively developed product, not a static database.

**The license constraint — read this before anything else:** the Data Suite Terms of Use (opened in this pass) state the charted play-by-play is proprietary/licensed IP; scraping or data-mining the site is expressly prohibited; **no commercial use, personal gain, or monetization without prior written consent**; and reposting data on social media requires attribution. Requests are rate-limited and metered per account, and they state they monitor social media for compliance.

**Lane fit — GSE (with the constraint applied):**
- ✅ *Internal research and signal validation* — cross-checking his engine's coverage/pressure/separation assumptions against human-charted ground truth. This is the single best external validation set for the charting-adjacent parts of GSE.
- ✅ *Attributed content* — the @FantasyPtsData bookmarks themselves are the model: their stat posts, reposted with attribution, are exactly what his X engagement operation already amplifies.
- ❌ *Commercial data feed* — the ToS forecloses piping this into a paid product, a paywalled pick service, or client deliverables without written consent. Any GSE monetization built on this data needs that consent first.

**Cost & effectiveness:** price UNVERIFIED in this pass — the subscribe flow routes through FantasyPoints sign-in, and no public page exposed the current Data Suite price. (Do not substitute PFF's or FantasyPros' prices; those are different products.) Effectiveness of the data itself is high: charted coverage/route/pressure data of this granularity is otherwise only available from PFF-grade vendors, and the charting team's pedigree (PFF process management, NFL team consulting) is documented on their own site.

**Launch steps:**
1. Subscribe via fantasypoints.com (the Data Suite homepage's subscribe link) — confirm the actual price at checkout before paying; it is Garrett's purchase either way.
2. First use: pull Week 1–4 coverage-shell and separation tables and diff them against the engine's current assumptions; log disagreements.
3. If any commercial use is ever contemplated, request written consent from Fantasy Points first — the ToS is explicit and they say they watch for violations.

### B5 · VoiceStudio — the "free open-source ElevenLabs replacement" (bookmark 6, @mikenevermiss, Sep 12)

**The item:** video post promoting a free, open-source ElevenLabs replacement — 19.4K GitHub stars, 646 languages, 14 TTS engines (post's numbers).

**Verified identity:** **VoiceStudio — github.com/debpalash/VoiceStudio.** Confirmed via GitHub API in this pass (live, 2026-10-13): **~62,500 stars, ~6,980 forks, AGPL-3.0, actively pushed (latest push the same day as this check).** (A 1-star same-name copy under another account also appears in search results; it is not the project.) The 646-language catalogue matches the post. The post's "19.4K stars" was accurate when posted in September — the repo has since blown up to roughly 3× that, which materially strengthens the adoption case. The current build ships **16 TTS engines and 11 ASR engines** (the post's "14 engines" reflects an earlier release — the project ships frequent releases).

**What it is & how it works:** a fully local desktop app (macOS/Windows/Linux/Docker) that bundles the workflows ElevenLabs charges for: zero-shot voice cloning from a short reference clip, voice design from a text description, video dubbing (transcribe → translate → preserve per-speaker voices → resynthesize → export), system-wide dictation, and multi-voice audiobook production (EPUB/PDF import, chapter rendering). Engines are swappable per job from a model catalogue; compute backends include CUDA, Apple Silicon MPS/MLX, ROCm, and CPU. It also exposes a local REST/SSE/WebSocket API, an OpenAI-compatible audio API, and an **MCP server** — meaning his agents can call it as a tool. Voices, projects, and outputs stay on the machine by default.

**Cost & effectiveness:**
- *Money:* $0. No account, no API key, no per-character billing — the entire ElevenLabs meter disappears. You supply the compute.
- *License caution:* the app is **AGPL-3.0**. Personal/internal use is unrestricted. If ARE ever ships it *as a network service* to clients, AGPL's network clause bites — run it locally per-client or get counsel; don't embed it in a hosted client product naively. Downloaded models keep their own upstream terms — check the specific cloning model's license before using a cloned voice commercially.
- *Effectiveness:* engine breadth is real (16 TTS engines is more than ElevenLabs exposes), but the 646-language figure is a catalogue claim — quality varies sharply by engine and language, per the project's own coverage notes. For English narration/VO (his actual use), the top engines are production-credible; for exotic languages, test before trusting. Local inference speed depends on his hardware; GPU strongly preferred for dubbing-length jobs.

**Lane fit:**
- *GSE (primary):* voiceover for GSE video content and narrated breakdowns without per-character API spend; the dictation workflow is a personal-efficiency bonus. The MCP server means a Dot/agent can generate VO as a pipeline step.
- *ARE:* a sellable capability for client content packages (podcast/VO/dubbing) at zero marginal cost — with the AGPL caveat above governing *how* it's deployed.

**Launch steps:**
1. Download the release build for his OS from the repo (or Docker) and install.
2. Record or select a 15-second clean reference clip of the target voice; build the clone.
3. A/B test: render the same 60-second script through VoiceStudio and ElevenLabs; judge blind.
4. If it passes, wire the MCP server into the agent stack and retire per-character VO billing for internal content.

*Also in this bookmark:* @mikenevermiss quoted his own Sep 11 post on **EvoMap AutoResearch** — dossiered below as B7.

### B7 · EvoMap AutoResearch (quoted inside bookmark 6; @mikenevermiss, Sep 11)

**What it is:** an open-source agent workflow (github.com/EvoMap/AutoResearch; EvoMap, "Infinite Evolution Lab") that takes AI/ML research ideas from hypothesis to *paper-ready evidence*. Launched Sept 1–2, 2026 (PR Newswire). Multiple models independently generate and cross-review ideas (minimum three distinct models in idea generation, so no model approves its own work); accepted ideas become executable research plans with defined metrics, success criteria, resource budgets, and evaluation procedures; specialized agents handle planning, implementation, experimentation, analysis, and review. State is persistent and recoverable — plans, code, run logs, metrics, *failures*, critic reports, and blind reviews are written to disk. Negative results are preserved and can terminate a line of inquiry instead of being argued away. Its stated premise: "a model's confidence is not evidence of success."

**Lane fit — GSE / personal research ops:** this is his own verification doctrine (build → measure → blind review → keep the negative results) packaged as open-source infrastructure. Direct uses: (1) the standing arXiv/NGS research program — idea generation from recent papers plus executed, evidence-logged follow-ups; (2) engine hypothesis testing (a proposed signal becomes a plan with pre-registered success criteria instead of a vibe). It slots beside, not instead of, his Jules/subagent lanes.

**Cost & effectiveness:** software is free/open-source; the real cost is model API spend across at least three models plus experiment compute — budget per research run, pilot before scaling (the workflow itself supports pilot-then-scale). Effectiveness: the *design* is sound and unusually honest about failure modes (self-validation, inflated self-evaluation), but all public evidence is the project's own; no independent benchmark exists yet. Treat as a promising pilot, not a proven platform.

**Launch steps:**
1. Clone EvoMap/AutoResearch; run its idea-generation path on one bounded GSE question (e.g., a single candidate signal family).
2. Inspect the evidence package end-to-end: plan, logs, critic report, blind review.
3. Compare against the same question run through his current research pipeline on quality-per-dollar; adopt only if it wins.

## Part 4 — Likes

### L3 · @Dan1ro0 (Sep 13) — "Bayesian Quant model" Polymarket claims — FULL VERDICT

**The claim:** a Bayesian quant model trading Polymarket BTC Up/Down markets makes $1,362/day, +$29,972 PnL in 22 days, on $29 average trades; the post quotes Dan1ro0's own Aug 19 article, "Top 10 Polymarket Trading Bots."

**Verdict: UNVERIFIED marketing. Do not allocate capital on this.**

Three independent reasons:
1. **No evidence, only assertion.** The PnL figures are self-reported in a post whose function is to promote the author's own listicle. No audited track record, no wallet address offered for verification, no third-party coverage exists. In this niche, unverifiable PnL screenshots are the standard affiliate-funnel format.
2. **The math strains credulity.** $1,362/day on ~$29 average position size implies either enormous trade frequency at a sustained edge or position sizes far larger than stated. Sustained edges of that size in the most competitive short-dated crypto markets on earth — against professional market makers — are not a thing a listicle author gives away.
3. **The regime changed underneath exactly these markets.** Verified from multiple independent sources in this pass: Polymarket introduced **dynamic taker fees on 5- and 15-minute crypto markets in January 2026** (fee peaks at roughly **1.56% at a 50¢ price**, using a probability-based formula), **removed the 500ms taker delay on February 18, 2026** (killing the latency window taker bots exploited), and extended dynamic fees platform-wide on March 30, 2026. BTC Up/Down is precisely the fee-bearing category. A taker strategy now needs **more than ~1.56% edge at mid prices just to break even**; the documented 2026 meta is the opposite side — makers pay zero fees and earn rebates funded by taker fees. Any BTC Up/Down bot pitch that doesn't lead with its fee math is selling the pre-2026 world.

**Lane fit:** none as a product. Its only value is as a labeled specimen in his research corpus: *how prediction-market bot marketing reads, and why the fee regime is the first question.* If he ever tests Polymarket systematically, the maker-side literature (post-Feb-2026 bot guides) is the starting point, not this.

### L7 · @0xCarnagee (Aug 25) — SpaceXAI engineer 1-hour workshop: Grok 4.6 in Cursor + GrokBot team workflow

**The item:** a workshop walkthrough with a SpaceXAI engineer covering Grok 4.6 in Cursor and the GrokBot team workflow — token spend, harness engineering, model amnesia, building agents.

**Corroborated context (opened sources):** the workshop's themes match SpaceXAI's own documented practices from its support-ops deployment: staged autonomy ("crawl, walk, run" — read-only with mandatory human sign-off first, escalation gated by ticket class), a retrieval-then-reason pipeline with a cost gate (cheap paths for known problems before expensive inference — the choice credited with making their reported per-resolution cost plausible), and persistent memory treated as a managed risk ("model amnesia" is the failure mode their harness engineering exists to prevent — bots keep changing facts in authoritative source systems, keep summaries in memory). Grok 4.6/4.7 were trained to natively understand the Grok Bot harness, which is why the team workflow demos run in Cursor.

**Lane fit — personal efficiency (fleet doctrine):** this is a free masterclass in running the exact kind of multi-agent operation he runs. The portable lessons: (1) cost-gate before reasoning — route known problem classes through cheap retrieval first; (2) staged autonomy with approval boundaries that loosen only by class, never globally; (3) memory hygiene — authoritative facts live in source systems, bots hold pointers and preferences. All three are directly applicable to his OpenDots/fleet review practices at zero cost.

**Cost & effectiveness:** free to absorb; the workshop content is practitioner-grade (the team's own deployment), though headline outcome numbers remain company-reported. **Launch steps:** none — doctrine extraction only; fold the three lessons into the fleet's standing rules alongside L6's field-notes adoption.

### L8 · @coreyganim (Aug 26) — Composio connected to Grok Bot for 1,000+ integrations

**What Composio is (verified):** a managed integration layer for AI agents — 1,000+ app toolkits (Gmail, Slack, Notion, Linear, HubSpot, Stripe, etc.) with managed OAuth (connect flow, token refresh, per-user scoping handled by Composio), exposed via Python/TypeScript SDKs, a CLI, and a managed MCP gateway that plugs into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or any MCP client. The "hack" in the post is simply: point Grok Bot (or any agent) at Composio's MCP endpoint and the agent wakes up able to act in 1,000+ apps without hand-built connectors.

**Pricing (verified from Composio's own published material and multiple independent 2026 breakdowns):** Free tier $0 — 20,000 tool calls/mo per Composio's own pricing article (some third-party listings after August 2026 cite a raised 100K free allowance; the discrepancy is flagged, the conservative 20K figure is the one to plan on); **$29/mo — 200,000 calls**; **$229/mo — 2,000,000 calls**; overage ≈ $0.25–$0.30 per 1K calls; Enterprise custom (adds VPC/self-host, SSO/SCIM, contractual SOC 2/ISO coverage). The full app catalog is available at every tier — the gate is call volume, not apps.

**The structural caveat:** on free/paid tiers, your OAuth credentials and tokens live in **Composio's cloud** — the trust boundary moves from your machine to their infrastructure. Fully self-hosted deployment is Enterprise-only. Their stated posture (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, encryption in transit/at rest) is vendor-claimed. For low-sensitivity automations that's a fine trade; for anything touching money movement, client credentials, or his core accounts, use minimum scopes and bring-your-own-OAuth where supported — or keep the direct-API path.

**Lane fit:**
- *ARE (primary):* this is the fastest way to give client-facing agents real app access (Gmail/CRM/scheduling) without building OAuth plumbing per client — days of integration work compressed to an afternoon, at $0–29/mo per deployment scale he's operating at.
- *GSE/personal:* useful for fleet plumbing (agent → Sheets/Notion/Gmail), but his existing direct connectors already cover the core; adopt where a *new* app appears, not as a wholesale replacement.

**Launch steps:**
1. Create a free Composio account; connect one low-stakes app (e.g., a test Gmail or Notion).
2. Attach the MCP gateway to one agent (Claude Code or a Dot) and run a read-only task end-to-end.
3. Audit the tool-call log; only then widen scopes. Budget trigger: move to $29/mo when free calls actually run out, not before.

## ALTITUDE — the created metric, methodology VERIFIED from stats.mockingboard.app/glossary/altitude
- What: weekly score for QB/RB/WR/TE = a historical percentile 0–100 against every qualifying game at the position since 2016. Bands: Grounded <10, Turbulence <40, Level <60, Cruising <90, Soaring ≥90. 50 = median.
- QB formula: EPA per dropback with the least reliable outcomes priced out — interception plays re-priced at that season's mean incompletion value (a single game of INTs is ~1% signal); sack fumbles priced as clean sacks.
- WR/TE/RB formula: EARNED yards — targets priced at the league rate for their depth; carries at the league rate for their box count. "Opportunity earned is the player; weekly conversion is mostly context and luck, so conversion is priced, never observed."
- Ingredient selection: split-half method — split a player's snaps at random, compute candidate stats on each half, keep only stats that agree with themselves inside one game.
- Qualifying gates: QB 15+ dropbacks; WR/TE 10+ routes; RB 8+ touches; regular season only.
- Published data views: qb_altitude_week / rb_altitude_week / wr_altitude_week / te_altitude_week with raw inputs beside the score (QB view carries raw AND de-noised EPA/dropback; receivers carry earned vs delivered yards). Explore at /explore.
- Measured reliability: single-game QB 0.147 (vs 0.099 passer rating, 0.109 raw EPA/dropback); TE 0.449; WR 0.356 (vs 0.267 raw yards); RB 0.307 (vs 0.201 delivered scrimmage yards). QB score reaches half signal in ~6 games. Their own words: "Even the best weekly number is mostly weather."
- Design rule: "delete provable luck, never add identity." An early composite leaning on rushing identity was discarded after it ranked an MVP season 22nd at the position (their "absurdity test").
- Stated limits: adjacent bands are often noise ("the band is the claim"); receiver Altitude grades opportunity earned, not catch outcomes; can't see pass-protection assignments, untargeted coverage, or pre-snap gravity.
- Related metrics on the card: EPA per dropback, CPOE, EPA (nflverse play-by-play).

## Theme 1 — Game State & Leverage (10 records)

### Record 1.1 — @EaglesXsandOs — 4 Feb 2025
- Source: https://x.com/EaglesXsandOs/status/1886882341584560226
- Post: EPA does not reweight for opponent or in-game situation. Key line: "a 10-yard gain from the 25-yard line in a tie game vs. the Chiefs in the 4th Quarter is weighted the same as in the 3rd Q of a 35-point blowout vs. the Panthers." Follow-up: "Not all 5 yard gains are created equally."
- THE SITUATION: A 10-yard gain, scored by EPA.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Score margin, quarter, and opponent strength. A tie game in Q4 vs Kansas City is a high-leverage snap; the same gain in a 35-point blowout vs Carolina is near-zero leverage. Flat EPA scores them identically.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Separate EPA (point value of the state change) from leverage/WPA (what the state change is worth in win probability). Weight plays by game state when the target is winning or team strength, not by yards or raw EPA alone.

### Record 1.2 — @ScottKacsmar — 3 Jan 2025
- Source: https://x.com/ScottKacsmar/status/1875030492480692271
- Post: "The sneak TD can be +0.03 on 1st down up to +3.45 (!) on 4th down." A 4-yard gain on 1st-and-10 at your own 30 can be about −0.05 EPA; a 5-yard gain on 2nd-and-6 can also be negative.
- THE SITUATION: Short-yardage gains near the goal line and on early downs.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The down. The finisher on a late down absorbs credit the early-down runners created; early-down gains below the success baseline can be negative EPA even while gaining yards.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: The price of a yard is set by down and distance. Never credit a play's yards without the state it started in; short-of-the-sticks gains late in a series are worth far more than the same yards early.

### Record 1.3 — @zxcvbnmwill — 6 Mar 2026
- Source: https://x.com/zxcvbnmwill/status/2029984303828947170
- Post: 3rd-and-4 from your own 45 is about 1.53 expected points; 1st-and-10 at the 50 is about 2.69, "so a 6 yard play is worth 1.16 EPA."
- THE SITUATION: A 6-yard gain on 3rd down.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The gain converts the down. Its value is EP(after) − EP(before) = 1.16, not "6 yards."
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Value is the change in state, not the yardage. Any feature built on raw yards without the before/after state is measuring the wrong thing.

### Record 1.4 — @galenhall — 29 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/galenhall/status/2104758740624797737
- Post: "Starting on your own 2 yard line is worth −.65, starting on your 31 … is worth 1.51." From the 2, even a failed 4th down gains about 2.16 expected points of field position — "almost as much as making the field goal" — so roughly a 17% TD rate breaks even.
- THE SITUATION: A drive starting inside your own 5; a 4th-down decision near your own goal line.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Field position is nonlinear. The failure state (opponent pinned deep after your failed attempt, or you after a punt exchange) is itself valuable, which crushes the break-even conversion rate far below 50%.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Near the goal lines, price the failure state, not just the conversion. Red-zone and backed-up states need their own baselines; a flat model mis-ranks both plays and decisions there.

### Record 1.5 — @ArkansasQuant — 11 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/ArkansasQuant/status/2109155529931280671
- Post: Late, one-score, 4th-and-long: teams that went for it won 9% of the time, 17% when starting in their own territory. Teams that punted won 2–7%, "depending on timeouts and clock."
- THE SITUATION: Late-game 4th-and-long, down one score.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The alternative's win rate. 9% sounds hopeless until the punt's 2–7% is next to it; timeouts and clock move both numbers.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Evaluate decisions by the delta versus the alternative, never by the absolute success rate. Leverage is a gap, not a level.

### Record 1.6 — @BenjaminSolak — 4 Nov 2024
- Source: https://x.com/BenjaminSolak/status/1853242268800733468
- Post: Overtime, 4th-and-1: the Next Gen Stats model recommended Seattle go — "The increase in win probability was 14.5%." "That's an enormous delta. It was an obvious go spot."
- THE SITUATION: 4th-and-1 in overtime.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Overtime compresses the state space — possessions are the game. A fast opponent score afterward is evidence FOR going (the punt would have surrendered the same possession), not against it.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Judge decisions by the ex-ante WP delta (+14.5%), not by the outcome that followed. Resulting is a training-data poison: a correct go that fails is still a correct go.

### Record 1.7 — @Timo_NFL — 21 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/Timo_NFL/status/2112794793772192033
- Post: Down 3 at the 2 with 1 second left collapses to immediate win or loss, versus a kick that sends you to overtime. A strong team converting ~51% might still prefer OT at ~55%; a bad defense flips it. Separate case: up 4, 4th down, 2:30 left, opponent out of timeouts — a field goal leaves a live game; a conversion can end it.
- THE SITUATION: Endgame 4th-down choices at both ends — trailing at the goal line, and leading late.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Team strength and defensive quality flip the preferred branch; timeouts determine whether the "safe" kick actually ends the game or hands the ball back.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Edge states (1 second left, kneel-out clocks, OT) are separate regimes, not the tail of the mid-game distribution. The same nominal choice is a different decision depending on which team you are.

### Record 1.8 — @bburkeESPN — 8 Sep 2025
- Source: https://x.com/bburkeESPN/status/1965115599228637192
- Post: "If you have a game state of score, time, down, distance, etc 's', then WP(s) tells you the chance of winning given that state." Going for it is an expected value: success probability × WP after success, plus failure probability × WP after failure.
- THE SITUATION: Any 4th-down (or two-point) decision.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The decision is an expectation over branches, not a conversion-rate lookup.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Decision rule — compute p × WP(success) + (1−p) × WP(failure) and compare it to WP(kick/punt). "Punt" is never a default; it is one branch among three, priced like the others.

### Record 1.9 — @tejfbanalytics — 15 Jan 2023
- Source: https://x.com/tejfbanalytics/status/1614654125316407301
- Post: One game, cumulative leverage: the Chargers had −13.1% win probability added on 4th downs, "mostly from kicking FG's on 4th-and-goal from the +4, 4th-and-goal from the +5 and 4th-and-3 from the +22." The Jaguars had +24.0% by staying aggressive.
- THE SITUATION: A single playoff game's worth of 4th-down decisions.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Individually "safe" kicks compounded into −13.1% WPA. Decision quality is visible in the sum, not in any one call's outcome.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Track cumulative decision WPA. A coach/team decision tendency is a measurable, persistent quantity — small per-play leaks are a real signal, not noise.

### Record 1.10 — @nfl4thbot — 19 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/nfl4thbot/status/2111977339873620380
- Post: Dallas, 4th-and-4 at the Green Bay 47, Q1 12:01, 0–0: coaches were predicted to punt (85%), but the model's pick was go for it, at +4.0% win probability.
- THE SITUATION: A neutral, early, scoreless 4th-and-medium at midfield.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Leverage exists in the first quarter too. +4.0% WP in Q1 is the same kind of object as +14.5% in overtime, at lower magnitude.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Do not treat early-game decisions as low-stakes by default. Price every 4th down in WP; the coach's conservative lean is not evidence the model is wrong.

### Theme 1 teaching points (from Grok's extraction)
- State, not the box score, is the unit: a play's worth is WP(after) − WP(before), or EP(after) − EP(before).
- Split expected points from win probability: down/distance/yard line set EP; score margin, clock, timeouts, quarter set how points convert to WP.
- Garbage time should be down-weighted for "who is good," not deleted from play value.
- Edge states break average models: kneel-out, 1-second-left, and overtime are not the same distribution as mid-game plays.

## Theme 2 — Game Script (12 records)

### Record 2.1 — @dwainmcfarland — 24 Oct 2022
- Source: https://x.com/dwainmcfarland/status/1584361724123447296
- Post: The Falcons trailed by 7+ on every snap and still dropped back on only 45% of plays, versus a league average of 72% in that spot.
- THE SITUATION: A team trailing all game, and its pass rate.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The league's script response (72%) is a baseline, not a law. This offense refused the script — team philosophy is a separate parameter from score state.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Learn a team-specific offset from the script-conditioned expectation. Score changes the play call in a predictable direction, but the size of the shift is a team trait.

### Record 2.2 — @LateRoundQB — 20 Nov 2017
- Source: https://x.com/LateRoundQB/status/932714807576399873
- Post: Lions and Vikings ranked top-10 in pace in a neutral game script (margin within 6). The Lions had the highest pass-to-rush ratio in football in that neutral script (1.93).
- THE SITUATION: Comparing team pace and pass tendency.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The comparison is only meaningful inside neutral script. Neutral script is the identity baseline; everything else is score effects.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Estimate pace, pass rate, and efficiency in close games first (margin within ~6, or WP roughly 20–80%). That is the team prior; extreme scripts are a separate state.

### Record 2.3 — @grok — 13 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/grok/status/2110143602475090202
- Post: Chargers at −8.6 PROE (3rd-most run-oriented). Raw split was almost even (147 rushes, 144 passes), but they had been trailing often, so the negative PROE means they ran more than the situations called for.
- THE SITUATION: A near-50/50 raw run/pass split.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: They trailed often, when the expected split tilts heavily pass. Raw rate and script-adjusted rate tell opposite stories about the same team.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Train on residuals versus expected pass rate given score, down, and distance (PROE), not on raw attempt shares. (Provenance note: this post is from X's own AI account summarizing the metric — treat as a secondary source.)

### Record 2.4 — @PurpyNFL — 17 Nov 2025
- Source: https://x.com/PurpyNFL/status/1990414391620125139
- Post: Vikings posted a −14% pass rate over expected. With that same game script, historical teams would have passed a lot more.
- THE SITUATION: A box score that looks pass-heavy.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Conditioned on the script they actually faced, they were run-heavy. The box score and the script-adjusted read point in opposite directions.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Any feature built from attempt counts must be script-adjusted before it enters a model, or it encodes the schedule of scores the team happened to face.

### Record 2.5 — @PurpyNFL — 8 Dec 2025
- Source: https://x.com/PurpyNFL/status/1998052431138074861
- Post: Vikings' PROE was 0% in one game, meaning they were more pass-happy than their own recent baseline once script was accounted for. Kneel-downs and sack/scramble coding also distort raw run/pass counts.
- THE SITUATION: A single game's run/pass accounting.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Coding artifacts — kneels, sacks, scrambles — move the raw count without reflecting a play call.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Exclude or reclassify kneel-downs, sacks, and scrambles before estimating script effects or team tendencies.

### Record 2.6 — @bjT98504 — 16 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/bjT98504/status/2100272656029278660
- Post: When leading, teams run more. Clock-killing 2-yard runs are low-EPA, so a defense can look fine in EPA while giving up large rush totals in lead-protection scripts.
- THE SITUATION: A defense's rushing yards allowed vs its EPA allowed.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Leading runs are a different play type — low-EPA by design. The two defensive metrics diverge when opponents spend long stretches protecting a lead.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Condition run-defense evaluation on score and leverage, or the ranking will track opponent script rather than defensive quality.

### Record 2.7 — @Moneylinehacks — 1 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/Moneylinehacks/status/2105472478789472359
- Post: Rushing volume and covering the spread move together because leading teams run. A back's yardage and his team's side of the score are not independent.
- THE SITUATION: Correlating a running back's volume with team success.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The causality runs through the scoreboard. Leaders run more; the carries are partly an effect of winning, not a cause.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Do not treat rush or pass attempts as exogenous inputs when predicting points, spreads, or player yardage. Volume and team success are jointly determined by script.

### Record 2.8 — @LinkofSunshine — 28 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/LinkofSunshine/status/2104659075506270564
- Post: Teams pass more when they are losing, which is why naive correlations between pass volume and outcomes break.
- THE SITUATION: A naive pass-volume/outcome correlation.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Script is a confounder, not noise. The losing causes the passing at least as much as the passing relates to losing.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Any pass-volume feature must carry the score state with it, or the model will learn the arrow of causality backwards.

### Record 2.9 — @hawkblogger — 17 Oct 2025
- Source: https://x.com/hawkblogger/status/1979308402619867353
- Post: Seahawks had the 2nd-fewest plays in the NFL when trailing, but led the league at 8.7 yards per play and a 9.0% TD rate on those 89 plays.
- THE SITUATION: A team's efficiency while trailing.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The sample is 89 plays — small, desperate, against defenses that have changed shape. Extreme trailing efficiency is not interchangeable with neutral-script efficiency.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Shrink extreme-script rates hard when a team rarely trails or rarely leads. Never pool trailing EPA with leading EPA.

### Record 2.10 — @NFLSnapIQ — 8 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/NFLSnapIQ/status/2108207509727023254
- Post: A very low early-down PROE may be real philosophy or just score and injuries. The useful split is neutral-game-script only.
- THE SITUATION: Interpreting a low early-down pass rate over expected.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Without the neutral-script split, scheme and circumstance are indistinguishable.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: The neutral-script early-down split is the diagnostic view. Build it before drawing any conclusion about coaching philosophy.

### Record 2.11 — @BAI8app — 11 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/BAI8app/status/2109371470493155784
- Post: A lopsided PROE is more about coaching than matchup until you split neutral-script early downs from the rest.
- THE SITUATION: A season-total PROE number.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The season total is a mixture of regimes weighted by how often the team was in each. Matchup, scheme, and script are blended.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Do not average across states. Reweight to a common script distribution before ranking teams or feeding a predictive feature.

### Record 2.12 — @RoyRobi73192051 — 11 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/RoyRobi73192051/status/2098428592409465260
- Post: Plain statement of the base rule: teams pass more when playing from behind.
- THE SITUATION: The foundational script regularity.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: None — this is the prior the other records refine.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Encode the base rule as the expectation; measure every team and game as a deviation from it.

### Theme 2 teaching points (from Grok's extraction)
- Pace is endogenous to the score: trailing speeds the game up, leading slows it down. Play counts and target opportunity are outcomes of script, not fixed inputs.
- Defense scheme is a function of score too: protecting a lead invites lighter boxes and softer coverage; chasing a deficit invites stacked boxes and pressure.
- A season-long pass rate, rush total, or EPA/play is a mixture of neutral, leading, and trailing regimes — reweight before comparing.

## Theme 3 — Situational Splits (12 records)

### Record 3.1 — @SharpFootball — 13 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/SharpFootball/status/2110075345227370707
- Post: Red-zone touchdown rate this season ranges from 87.5% (San Francisco) to 42.9% (Chicago), with most teams clustered between roughly 50% and 70%.
- THE SITUATION: A drive reaching the opponent's 20.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The red zone is a separate state with huge team dispersion. The same offense that moves the ball between the 20s can be a bottom-tier finisher.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Define the red zone as its own state (inside the 20, goal-to-go nested inside it) and score the drive outcome — TD vs FG vs nothing — separately from the yards earned getting there.

### Record 3.2 — @GridironInfo_ — 15 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/GridironInfo_/status/2110788330166083977
- Post: Defines red-zone efficiency as EPA per play once inside the opponent's 20. In 2026, San Francisco's offense was the most efficient there; Jacksonville's defense the stingiest.
- THE SITUATION: Measuring red-zone performance.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Per-play efficiency inside the 20 is a different quantity from season-long EPA; the leaderboard does not carry over.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Keep red-zone EPA as a split feature for both offense and defense; never let full-field EPA stand in for it.

### Record 3.3 — @SharpFootball — 13 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/SharpFootball/status/2110064523553972365
- Post: Baltimore early downs in the red zone: +0.67 EPA per dropback (4th) and +0.32 per rush (4th). On 3rd down in field-goal range: −0.57 EPA per play, worst in the NFL.
- THE SITUATION: One team's situational splits.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Early-down red-zone strength and 3rd-down field-goal-range failure coexist in the same offense. The down split reverses the conclusion.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Within the red zone, split by down. An aggregate red-zone number can hide the exact down where the offense breaks.

- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Between-the-20s explosives flattered the offense; inside the 20 it is near the league's worst on every measure.

### Record 3.5 — @dmlr53 — 29 Sep 2026

- Post: Starting a drive inside your own 5 carries about −0.5 to −0.8 expected points. A failed conversion there hands the opponent a far better state than the raw yards suggest.

- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The starting state is already negative. A 30-yard gain from the own 10 is worth less than a short-yardage score from midfield.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Backed-up is a negative-EP state; value plays from it in EP/EPA, never raw yards, or the model overvalues empty yardage from bad field position.

### Record 3.6 — @officialctpod — 28 Dec 2024

- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Fourth-down conversion priors must be era-current and distance-specific; stale priors systematically under-price going for it.

- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Treat distance-to-go as a first-class, continuous feature on 3rd/4th down. "Long" is a probability, not a verdict.

- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: State the WP band any EPA feature was computed on (common operational garbage-time definitions: WP outside ~5–95% or ~10–90%, or 17+ down in Q4). Rankings without the filter definition are not comparable.

- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The state changed mid-window. What began as clock management re-entered a live, high-leverage problem.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: States are dynamic. A large point swing in a short window moves the game out of the prevent regime — re-classify the state instead of averaging the whole stretch as "garbage time."

- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The compressed field changes the completion/TD/INT profile completely versus his open-field numbers; the split, not the aggregate, describes how he plays where it tightens.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Player efficiency features must be state-split. A QB's red-zone TD/INT profile is a separate quantity from his overall line and can diverge sharply.

### Theme 3 teaching points (from Grok's extraction)
- Prevent defense inflates volume and suppresses explosives: yards and completions against prevent overstate offensive quality; down-weight them, and weight scoring rate and explosive rate instead.
- Leverage-adjusted EPA (plays that can still swing the game count more) is more predictive than raw EPA.
- Production against backups in a blowout should not update a player or team prior at full weight.

## Theme 4 — Coaching Decisions in Context (8 records)

### Record 4.1 — @RyanPaganetti — 21 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/RyanPaganetti/status/2112949460733165950
- Post: Facing 4th-and-2.5 in a tie from their own 46 with about 2 minutes left, the Ravens took a delay of game and punted. ESPN graded it an 8.6-point win-probability mistake. Converting would win ~71%, failing ~29%; estimated conversion odds 55–60%, so going for it was roughly a 55% win chance vs about 46% for the punt.
- THE SITUATION: Tie game, ~2:00 left, 4th-and-short at midfield.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Trusting the defense does not flip the call — a failed attempt still leaves paths to win, while a conversion makes them heavy favorites. The delay-of-game penalty was a decision cost on top of the punt itself.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Price the full WP of go vs punt with branch values (WP after success ≈ 71%, after failure ≈ 29%), not conversion rate alone. A modest conversion chance still wins when the alternative hands the opponent a favored drive.

### Record 4.2 — @BenjaminSolak — 11 Nov 2024
- Source: https://x.com/BenjaminSolak/status/1855833141803372852
- Post: Texans tied 23–23, 4th-and-4 on the Lions' 40, 1:56 remaining. Next Gen Stats win probability: punt 41%, field-goal attempt 39%, go for it 52%. "Was a clear go spot. Big error late for the Texans."
- THE SITUATION: Tie game, under 2 minutes, 4th-and-4 in opponent territory.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: All three branches priced: the kick was actually the worst option (39%), below even the punt. "Safe" and "correct" diverged by 13 points of WP.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Always price all three branches. In long-field-goal range late in a tie, the field goal can be dominated by both alternatives.

### Record 4.3 — @billbarnwell — 8 Sep 2024
- Source: https://x.com/billbarnwell/status/1832911439561982390
- Post: "This punt has basically gone out of the game — trailing by one TD or less on fourth-and-1 from the opponent's 40–49 yard line, teams have gone for it 63 out of 64 times over the last five years."
- THE SITUATION: 4th-and-1, opponent's 40–49, trailing by one score or less.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The league's revealed base rate in this exact narrow bin is 63/64 go. A punt here is a 1-in-64 outlier, not a judgment call.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Historical base rates in narrow state bins are strong priors. When a coach deviates from a near-unanimous bin, the burden of proof is on the deviation.

### Record 4.4 — @NextGenStats — 10 Jan 2022
- Source: https://x.com/NextGenStats/status/1480383946718203905
- Post: Chargers' decision to go for it on 4th-and-1 from their own 18 was optimal on the NGS Decision Guide: win % if go 36%, if punt 35%, recommendation go by 1.4%.
- THE SITUATION: 4th-and-1 from your own 18 — the deepest "never go" territory in conventional wisdom.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Field position thresholds are not absolute. When the punt's expected net is small, even a backed-up 4th-and-1 can be a (slight) go.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: No state is categorically off-limits to the EV computation. Compute the branches everywhere; let the numbers, not field-position folklore, draw the lines.

### Record 4.5 — @BenjaminSolak — 10 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/BenjaminSolak/status/2097885845046919677
- Post: Next Gen Stats called 4th-and-9 from the opponent's 47 a strong go. "If you punt, you need to force a 3-and-out to get the ball back. If you go for it and fail… you need to force a 3-and-out to get the ball back anyway."
- THE SITUATION: 4th-and-9, late, needing the ball back.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The defensive requirement after a punt and after a failed attempt is the same (a 3-and-out). The punt buys almost nothing except worse field position on the failure branch.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: When both branches require the same defensive outcome, the go branch weakly dominates. Compare what each branch actually changes, not the labels "aggressive" vs "safe."

### Record 4.6 — @MikeReiss — 11 Sep 2023
- Source: https://x.com/MikeReiss/status/1701068291953823848
- Post: Belichick going for it on 4th-and-3 from the Eagles' 17, trailing 22–14 with 9:39 left, agreed with by ESPN Analytics: WP going for it 21.4%, kicking 20.8%.
- THE SITUATION: Down 8, 9:39 left, 4th-and-3 at the opponent's 17.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Inside the red zone the kick is nearly automatic points, yet the go still edged it — because down 8, the touchdown's value toward tying outweighs the certain 3.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Score margin interacts with the kick/go choice: a field goal that leaves you still trailing by two scores is worth less than its points. Model the margin after each branch, not just the points.

### Record 4.7 — @Timo_NFL — 21 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/Timo_NFL/status/2112794822490612072
- Post: 4th down, 2:30 left, no opponent timeouts, up by 4. Kick a field goal to go up 7 and play defense (OT if they score), or go for it and end the game immediately a significant share of the time.
- THE SITUATION: Leading by 4 late, opponent out of timeouts, 4th down in field-goal range.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The field goal does not end the game — it creates a new one (a tying drive, then OT). The conversion ends it on the spot a meaningful fraction of the time.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Score, clock, and opponent timeouts interact. "Take the points" is not a terminal state; price the game that follows the kick.

### Record 4.8 — @nfl4thbot — 19 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/nfl4thbot/status/2111977339873620380
- Post: DAL ball, 4th-and-4 at the GB 47, Q1 12:01, 0–0. Predicted coach action punt (85%), but the model's pick is go for it (+4.0% win probability).
- THE SITUATION: Scoreless first quarter, midfield, 4th-and-medium.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The model-vs-coach disagreement is itself quantified (+4.0% WP). Neutral early spots still carry decision leverage.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: A coach's conservative lean is not automatically justified by information the model lacks. Several-point WP edges are rarely overturned by personnel adjustments (backup QB, kicker form) alone — but personnel should still shift the conversion/make estimates that feed the calculation.

### Theme 4 teaching points (from Grok's extraction)
- "You need a stop either way" logic favors going when a failed attempt and a punt leave the same defensive requirement.
- Be careful at the edges of the state space (kneel-out clocks, very late, extreme deficits): models trained on typical plays can miscalibrate WP there, but the decision rule stays expected win probability.
- Gap noted: this theme returned almost entirely 4th-down material; timeout-management and challenge-specific breakdowns were barely represented in what X search surfaced.

## Theme 5 — Personnel & Matchup Context (10 records)

### Record 5.1 — @SharpFootball — 23 Jul 2020
- Source: https://x.com/SharpFootball/status/1286105755016474624
- Post: Of the eight personnel groupings used 100+ times, 21 personnel was the most efficient: #1 in yards/play, EPA/play, and success rate.
- THE SITUATION: Comparing efficiency across personnel groupings.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The heavy grouping (2 RB, 1 TE) tops the efficiency table — the opposite of the spread-era intuition — because of the defensive response it forces.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Personnel is a prior on the defensive response, not just an offensive label. Model the response (base vs nickel, box, shell) as part of the play's context.

### Record 5.2 — @Michael_Nania — 11 Dec 2023
- Source: https://x.com/Michael_Nania/status/1734198813202452612
- Post: Jets overused 11 personnel (league-worst ~3.9–4.0 yds/play). In one game they cut 11 to 41% and were far better in 12 (8.2 yds/play) and 21 (7.1). Season ranks: 11 personnel 32nd in yds/play; 12 and 21 both 10th.
- THE SITUATION: One offense, three personnel packages, opposite efficiency.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Personnel fit, not raw volume, drove expected output. The same players produced bottom-tier and top-10 results depending on the grouping.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Expected production is team-by-package specific. A single team efficiency number that ignores personnel mix blends away the actual signal.

### Record 5.3 — @Bumi_mind — 19 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/Bumi_mind/status/2112284080029241824
- Post: Dallas designed runs from 11: high usage, mediocre EPA (−0.05). Designed runs from 12: low usage, strong EPA (+0.09). Dropbacks reverse it: 11 top-8 EPA (+0.14), 12 bottom-5 (−0.23).
- THE SITUATION: One offense's run/pass value by personnel.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Run and pass value flip sign by package. "Dallas's offense" has no single EPA; it has a run-in-12 number and a pass-in-11 number.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Split run and pass expectations by package and encode the interaction. A personnel main effect without the run/pass interaction will be wrong in both directions.

### Record 5.4 — @sambruchhaus — 28 Apr 2026
- Source: https://x.com/sambruchhaus/status/2049241374826938696
- Post: Jaguars were strong passing in 11 and weak rushing. Moving to 12 did not improve pass EPA (unlike Jets +109% and Bills +33%) and crushed rush EPA (−450%). Defenses still played base at an above-average rate, but the secondary TEs were not real receiving threats, so the box could be loaded without a pass penalty.
- THE SITUATION: A team shifting to heavier personnel expecting a boost.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The extra TE's receiving threat is the moderator. Without it, defenses load the box for free; with it (Jets/Bills), the same shift creates a real tradeoff.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Condition on the receiving threat of TE2/FB (target rate, receiving grade), not just the personnel label. The label alone does not determine the defensive price.

### Record 5.5 — @JonnyPage9 — 21 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/JonnyPage9/status/2102122624965021893
- Post: The offense runs better from 11 when it spreads the defense. Heavy personnel, condensed formations, and runs into stacked boxes have not worked.
- THE SITUATION: Run-game efficiency by formation.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Formation width is part of the context. Spread 11 lightens the box the run faces; condensed heavy sets create the stacked box they then have to beat.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Expected rush value depends on personnel AND the box and width it creates. Include formation width (spread vs condensed) as a feature alongside personnel.

### Record 5.6 — @RyanPaganetti — 17 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/RyanPaganetti/status/2100388366009118844
- Post: Two-back looks (21/22-style) are a counter to two-high shells. Against middle-of-field-open coverages: +0.10 EPA/play on runs and +0.26 on passes, better than 2×2 or 3×1.
- THE SITUATION: An offense facing two-high / MOF-open shells.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The shell the defense wants to play has an offensive counter with a personnel answer. Heavier backfield personnel changes the shell the defense can safely play — and lifts both run and pass EPA against it.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Coverage shell is part of the same tradeoff as personnel. Predict shell from personnel (and vice versa), then predict EPA conditional on the shell.

### Record 5.7 — @HoodBall_15 — 20 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/HoodBall_15/status/2112540289432686906
- Post: Vs 11–12 personnel, three defensive problems: (1) box count and gap soundness at the point of attack, (2) extra gaps and edge control from a second TE, (3) coverage conflict — play-action, seams, and RPOs stop linebackers from fitting the run and covering hook/curl at the same time.
- THE SITUATION: A defense structuring against 11/12 personnel.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The second TE is not one more blocker; it creates extra gaps AND a coverage conflict for the same linebackers. The stress is structural, not a talent gap.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: The value of heavy personnel is partly the conflict it imposes, not the bodies themselves. Features should capture gap count and LB conflict, not only box count.

### Record 5.8 — @Kovb41 — 16 May 2026
- Source: https://x.com/Kovb41/status/2055695805458079931
- Post: When defenses loaded the box vs 13 personnel, pass EPA stayed above +0.21 in both 2024 and 2025. The same loaded-box look vs 11 fell from +0.18 to +0.04.
- THE SITUATION: Passing against a loaded box, by personnel.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Box count has no fixed effect. Loaded box vs 13 is a pass opportunity; loaded box vs 11 decayed toward neutral year over year.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Never use box count as a standalone feature. Its effect is an interaction with personnel and era; model it as such.

### Record 5.9 — @popofansports — 19 Oct 2026
- Source: https://x.com/popofansports/status/2111972583901925441
- Post: "Stacking the box" is often just matching heavy personnel (fewer WRs outside, more LBs, less two-deep), not an independent strategic choice — and it leaves the defense more vulnerable to the pass.
- THE SITUATION: A defense credited/blamed for stacking the box.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: The box was forced by the offense's declared personnel. The "choice" is largely a mirror, and its cost (pass vulnerability) is the real content.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Credit for beating a heavy box should be adjusted for whether the offense forced that box or simply declared heavy and ran into the natural response.

### Record 5.10 — @CaseL731 — 19 Sep 2026
- Source: https://x.com/CaseL731/status/2101123873500475827
- Post: Box count mostly reports the offense's personnel. Teams that rarely play three WRs will not see light boxes; treating box count as independent of 11/12/21 misstates the constraint.
- THE SITUATION: Using box count as a defensive-tendency feature.
- THE CONTEXT THAT CHANGES THE READ: Box count is endogenous to the offense's personnel distribution. A team that never spreads out never earns a light box to beat.
- THE LESSON FOR THE MODEL: Usage is endogenous — defenses price tendencies in. Residual EPA after conditioning on personnel, down-and-distance, and defensive response is closer to skill than raw EPA by personnel.

### Theme 5 teaching points (from Grok's extraction)
- Practical feature set: personnel code (11/12/21/13), formation width, box count relative to blockers, coverage family (two-high vs single-high, nickel vs base), and receiving threat of the extra TE/FB. Predict rush EPA, pass EPA, and target distribution jointly from that context.
- Two-high shells are attacked by two-back and heavier sets; base vs nickel changes who is in coverage (LBs vs DBs) and therefore expected completion and YAC by position.
