### D1 — @Timo_NFL — Playoff-leverage selection bias in dynamic-rating simulations (10-post thread, Oct 23)

**WHAT IT IS.** A methodological correction to a chart genre the whole industry publishes. Season simulations often update team ratings *inside* the simulation (a simulated Week 7 win raises the team's rating for simulated Weeks 8–18). If "playoff leverage" for this week's game is then computed by comparing playoff odds across sims filtered to wins vs sims filtered to losses, the number is inflated: the win-filter doesn't just select the game outcome, it also selects sims where the team drew a higher rating path — so the team wins more *future* games for reasons that have nothing to do with this game. His measurement for Week 7 games: the filter method inflates leverage by a factor of **1.3–1.6× per team**, with ~1.3 as the floor for any team still in the hunt. His published leverage chart corrects for this and shows the single-game effect only. His test: if a game truly doesn't matter, its leverage should be 0 — the filter method returns a positive number anyway, which proves the contamination.

**WHERE IT COMES FROM.** Timo Riske — verified as the author of PFF's playoff-picture series (PFF, 2021–2025), where playoff leverage is his signature chart and where his documented causal method is the *paired simulation*: copy each sim, flip only the game in question, and difference the outcomes. The thread is the same author explaining why the dynamic-ratings variant of the chart — used by other sim publishers — cannot be read at face value. Dynamic ratings exist for real reasons (they keep the sim from being overconfident off extreme current ratings, and the update factor K is a tuning lever), but they "do not necessarily reflect reality," and they poison the leverage filter.

**HOW TO USE IT / INPUTS.** Any Monte Carlo season sim with team ratings. Rule: compute leverage from paired/flipped sims or with ratings frozen at their pre-game values; never by outcome-filtering a dynamic-rating sim. The 1.3–1.6× factor is his measurement on his setup — the *mechanism* (conditioning on a post-outcome variable) is not in doubt, the exact factor is UNVERIFIED independently.

**WHICH LAYER.** Everything-else (season context / playoff picture) — and a standing audit question for any third-party sim output GSE cites, including the LineOfEvidence Sim Lab class of tools: *which leverage construction produced this number?*

**CREATIVE ANGLES.** If GSE ever publishes leverage or rooting-interest content, the paired-flip construction is the defensible one and the bias explanation is itself publishable reasoning — a "why the popular chart overstates this game by ~40%" explainer is exactly the reasoning-as-product genre. The same selection-bias pattern applies anywhere an outcome filter is applied to a path-dependent sim (DFS ownership sims, survivor WPs).

**RISKS.** Factor range is single-source (the author's own sims). Not a betting input by itself; it disciplines other inputs.

**VERDICT: LEARN-ONLY** (method doctrine). Posts: 2113646016050180154, 2113646652208697733, 2113646896611045690, 2113647404645842970, 2113647697907638421, 2113648290936045868, 2113648791995953370, 2113649441085493649, 2113654108272075166, 2113661482588422520.


### D2 — @PattonAnalytics — Play-Caller Evaluation Model v3.0 (Substack article read in full)

**Posts.** "Play Caller Tendencies 🎮" (Oct 22 — Declan Doyle 9th, Brad Idzik 11th ranked as first-time callers; David Blough 21st, Sean Mannion 29th), the tendency-vs-design follow-up, and the two "full breakdown of v3.0" posts linking the article (Oct 22).

**WHAT IT IS (verified at the primary source — pattonanalytics365.substack.com/p/evaluating-play-callers, "Evaluating Play Callers," Part III — Offense, published 2026-10-22).** A process-only play-caller rating built from six tendency components, deliberately *not* built from outcomes:
1. **Personnel diversification** — for every play, a model predicts the probability of 11/12/21/other personnel from the game situation; the component is the **Shannon entropy** of that distribution. Credit goes not for using many packages but for using them *without the situation giving them away*.
2. **Play-sequencing predictability** — whether the previous few calls predict the next call beyond what down/distance/score already explain.
3. **Play-sequencing volatility** — drive-to-drive variance of (2); two offenses can average the same predictability with very different shapes.
4. **PROE Plus** — pass rate over expectation combined with offensive pace (aggressiveness × tempo profile).
5. **Motion rate.**
6. **Play-action rate.**
The six are transformed, **oriented by their historical relationship to offensive EPA** (the "Y-aware" step — EPA is a compass, not an input), passed through **PCA**, weighted by variance explained, and combined into the rating. Callers are also grouped into four *style clusters*, explicitly not quality tiers. An "Easy Button %" (RPO + screen + play-action share) is computed but kept out of the score as a descriptive stat. Top of the board through Week 6: Shanahan and Reid; Payton near the top despite Denver's negative EPA/play — the author names that process/outcome gap as the model's point, not its flaw. His own limits, on the record: it is not a pure estimate of coaching value above replacement, it cannot see reads/protection adjustments/wrong routes, and the defensive version is exploratory only.

**HOW TO USE IT / INPUTS.** Play-by-play with personnel groupings (nflverse pbp carries personnel fields), down/distance/score state, and play-action flags (in nflverse). Motion rate is the one component needing charted data (Fantasy Points Data class) — five of six components are computable from public pbp. The sequencing components need a situation-conditioned call-prediction model (a multinomial model on state features; the residual predictability from recent-call features is the metric).

**WHICH LAYER.** Matchups — coach-vs-coach is an explicit signal family in GSE's reasoning doctrine, and this is the most fully specified public framework for the offensive half of it. Personnel entropy in particular is a matchup input GSE does not currently have: an offense whose personnel doesn't leak its intentions is harder to match up against, independent of its EPA.

**CREATIVE ANGLES.** (a) Build the 5-of-6 public approximation and compare its rankings to Patton's published tendencies posts as a validation target. (b) The entropy construction ports to defense: coverage-shell entropy given situation is the defensive mirror. (c) Sequencing predictability is a live in-game signal class (drive 1 vs drive 3 predictability drift) that no GSE layer currently touches.

**RISKS.** The Y-aware orientation can smuggle EPA back into a "process" score (the author acknowledges the tension); rankings beyond the article's named examples are UNVERIFIED; six-week samples; motion component is charted-data-gated.

**VERDICT: LEARN-ONLY.** Register-worthy. Gap: Parts I–II of the series (linked from Part III) were not read this pass.


### D3 — @MagicSportsGuy — aDOT is six different numbers (measurement-provenance post, Oct 20)

**WHAT IT IS.** One post that does more for data hygiene than most threads: JJ McCarthy's aDOT as published by six top sources — StatRankings **12.0**, PFR **12.0**, Sumer **14.76**, PFF **15.6**, Fantasy Points **11.57**, FTN **10.9**. A 4.7-yard spread on the same player and the same named stat, because each source's air-yards equation differs (which attempts count, how throwaways/spikes/behind-the-line throws are treated). His conclusion: "None of them are wrong; they are all run by sharp people, but they use slightly different equations (except PFR & StatRankings)" — PFR and StatRankings share the same equation, which is why they agree to the decimal. First-party note: the poster is StatRankings' own operator (see D4), so the StatRankings/PFR figures are first-party; the other four are as cited by him.

**WHICH LAYER.** All of them — this is the general form of the Oct 29 Catchable Ball Rate finding: *a charted stat is not a number, it is a number plus a definition plus a source.* Any external chart ingested into the engine (aDOT, catchable rate, pressure rate) needs its source pinned before its values can be compared or trended.

**CREATIVE ANGLES.** A standing "definition registry" for every external stat GSE ingests (source, equation notes, agreement class — e.g., PFR≡StatRankings) would convert this recurring surprise into a lookup. Cross-source spreads like this one are also a free data-quality alarm: when two sources in the same agreement class diverge, something changed upstream.

**VERDICT: LEARN-ONLY.** Post: 2112694980196303172.


### D4 — StatRankings platform, its AI connector, and its two-model provenance problem (posts Oct 20–23; site verified)

**Posts.** NBA projections launch (free all month), a McCarthy target-share breakdown produced "per the AI connector @StatRankings," the DFSArmy ownership partnership announcement, the Week 7 injury-summary format post, and the projections availability rule (all @MagicSportsGuy); plus three @PattonAnalytics replies disclosing model provenance.

**WHAT IT IS (verified at statrankings.com, fetched 2026-10-30).** A subscription data platform: 1,048 NFL stats, StatBuilder+, Coverage IQ+ (man/zone splits across all eight coverage shells; 132 WR coverage stats), custom splits, a 19-book odds board with vig removed, betting-trends back to 2000, and downloadable stat archives back to 2021 (CSV add-on $60/yr; standalone $179.99/yr; statrankings+ $34.99/mo or $139.99/yr). Founded by Kevin Adams; **Steven Patton (@PattonAnalytics) is its Data Scientist** — confirming the §6 Patton posts are first-party. The "AI connector" from the posts is real: a subscription unlocks a connector letting Claude/ChatGPT/Grok query the stat base (PDF connection guide after purchase; no API keys). Two operational rules disclosed in posts: DFS ownership projections are DFSArmy's, integrated into the projections tool at no extra cost; and the projection model's availability rule is mechanical — *two consecutive DNPs (Thu+Fri) = OUT in the model*, ahead of the official report, by design.

**THE PROVENANCE PROBLEM (from Patton's own replies in this pull).** Asked about a model output, he states: "This isn't the public model, it's StatRankings proprietary internal model," and "The model was designed back in February. I modified the public framework with two additional variables to account for game situation." So StatRankings numbers in the wild can come from either of two models, and the internal one is a modified version of a public framework plus two undisclosed game-situation variables. Not a scandal — a labeling fact: StatRankings-sourced model claims carry an unknowable model identity unless the post says which one.

**WHICH LAYER.** Data-source shelf for matchups/usage inputs; the AI-connector distribution pattern (a stat base sold as an LLM connector rather than a website) is also a direct competitive reference for GSE's own data products.

**VERDICT: WATCH** (platform). Posts: 2112603433077456999, 2112621956231245896, 2113682273187070446, 2113691595149377850, 2113747253483684122; provenance replies 2112652727104737640, 2112658683905921186, 2112660061931831790.


### D5 — @jmthrivept — injury prognosis by mechanism + historical comps (Batch D; method posts Oct 20–23)

**WHAT IT IS.** A physical therapist's injury-analysis practice, and the pull captures its two working methods:
1. **Historical-comp prognosis tables.** On Terry McLaurin's confirmed torn patellar tendon (Oct 20), he posts the comp set: David Boston (24 — next season 70-880-7 in 14 games, then tore the *other* patellar tendon in year 2), Victor Cruz (28 — missed the next season entirely to a calf injury during rehab, returned year 2 at 39-586-1 in 15 games), Jimmy Graham (29 — next season 65-923-6 in 16 games, year 2: 57-520-10), framing McLaurin at 31 against them.
2. **Mechanism reasoning.** Calf strains elevate Achilles-rupture risk through faulty force transmission (applied to the Rams' conservative RTP handling and Puka Nacua); a prior core/groin injury can make the nervous system redistribute load and alter activation timing, suppressing distal (calf) peak output — with the practical distinction that a neural re-activation problem can play this week while a true strain cannot (examples cited: Marshawn Lloyd, Christian Watson); plus a reporting-epistemics post: an initially mislabeled injury type propagates through the insider telephone chain and corrupts every downstream expectation (the Lamar Jackson case).

**VERIFICATION.** The comp table checks out where independently verifiable: Cruz's 2016 return line (39-586-1) and Graham's 2016 line (65-923-6) match the historical record as republished in SI's own Oct 2026 McLaurin history pieces and the standard comp tables; SI's coverage of the same injury cites a 2025 *Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine* study (45 NFL patellar-tendon tears; 57.8% returned to play; median return 11.4 months) — the account's method is the published clinical-historical method, executed accurately. His week-level availability leans (e.g., Lamar plays, Puka misses Week 7) are his stated opinion, labeled by him as "best medical education guess," and are graded as opinion here.

**WHICH LAYER.** Health — this is the input class the health layer actually needs: not in/out status but *mechanism, expected timeline, and reinjury pathway* per named player. The comp-table format is directly reusable as an engine artifact: injury → age-matched historical comps → distribution of outcomes, including the year-2 second-injury pattern (Boston) that a simple "returns in ~11 months" line hides.

**RISKS.** Single-operator medical opinion at social-media distance (no examinations); comp sets are small-n by nature; his fantasy-league asides are noise around the signal.

**VERDICT: LEARN-ONLY.** Posts: 2112624699847098817, 2112640237080039845, 2113686523099144227, 2113686857867571609, 2113705033141489864, 2113754973800640861, 2113755555177390467. (His remaining 28 pull posts are replies, availability notes, and chatter — cluster entry in Part 2.)


### D6 — @DynatyzeFF — Dynatyze metric suite and the WAR Board (Batch D; dynatyze.com verified)

**WHAT IT IS.** A fantasy-analytics product (dynatyze.com) publishing a family of named metrics in tier/list form: **RB Independent Creation** tiers (last-2-weeks leaders: Walker/Bijan/Warren tier 1), **Alpha Role** leaders (usage-role dominance; Mike Evans tier 1), TE **boom %** and **RZ Role**, route-participation lists — and the flagship **WAR Board**: positional fantasy WAR with "Field Graph" visualizations. The WAR definition is verified at the primary source (dynatyze.com/football/war-board, fetched 2026-10-30): *"wins added over the replacement player at a chosen league size, lineup and scoring format, from weekly positional finishes, for every season since 1999"* — free to view. The posts' Week 7 board: JSN the clear WR WAR leader; Gibbs/Walker III the top-2 RB race; Isaiah Likely the #1 TE (the breakout nobody predicted); Josh Allen far ahead at QB. And the board's most instructive output, which the account owns rather than hides: asked whether Parker Washington is really better than Ja'Marr Chase, the answer is "According to the board? Yes" — a replacement-level artifact (Washington's wins-added are inflated by availability and a low positional replacement bar), published with the artifact visible.

**WHAT'S NOT DEFINED.** Independent Creation, Alpha Role, boom %, and RZ Role formulas do not appear in the posts; the site's tape tool (dynatyze.com/football/tape, parameterized by position/week/column) exists, but this pass did not extract definitions for the four — they stay named-but-undefined, UNVERIFIED as constructions.

### D8 — @FantasyProsLabs — two first-party studies: ECR deviation cost, and absence-effect asymmetries (Oct 21–23)

**STUDY 1 — deviating from consensus costs more than it gains.** From millions of real synced lineups, Weeks 1–6: over half of all lineups differed from the "optimal" lineup implied by Expert Consensus Rankings. Of the start/sit decisions that went off-script, **55% lost points** versus the ECR choice (after removing lineups with injured/bye starters), and the asymmetry is in the magnitudes: losses averaged **−8.8 points**, gains **+7.1**. Status: FIRST-PARTY STATED — FantasyPros owns the lineup data and the ECR; the design is stated plainly and the numbers were not independently reproduced.

**STUDY 2 — "Fantasy Mythbusters Ep. I," every case 2018–25.** Three absence myths tested: (a) the star WR being out does **not** symmetrically boost the WR2 (no hypertargeting windfall in reverse); (b) without the WR2, the star WR1's target share rises only modestly — stars are already near their ceilings; (c) a backup QB does **not** hyper-target his WR1 — the WR1 keeps his share but scores **1.2 fewer points per game** because the whole offense degrades (worked example: CeeDee Lamb 2022 with Cooper Rush — share rose 26%→37% and he *still* lost 2.5 ppg).

**WHICH LAYER.** Usage — this is the correction term for the engine's role-shift logic (Session 3's C-301 role shift alerts): the naive adjustment "absent player's share flows to the next man" is empirically wrong in both directions; the offense-level degradation term dominates the share-transfer term for QB changes.

### D13 — @ihartitz — the Mismatch Manifesto's additive matchup index (Oct 22)

**WHAT IT IS.** A weekly chart series built on one transparent construction: for each matchup stat, publish a **single combined number = the offense's rate + the defense's allowed rate** — combined EPA/play, combined yards before contact per rush ("Kyren Williams + Blake Corum boom weeks?" is what a high combined YBC looks like), plus combined explosive pass/run rates, pressure, and yards per dropback. Data: TruMedia, 2026 season only. His stated purpose: "One metric to show a mismatch instead of going 'Offense ranks x, defense ranks y.'"

**ASSESSMENT.** An additive matchup index: honest, reproducible from any pbp source (the YBC variant needs charted/tracking data; the EPA variant is pure nflverse), and deliberately simple — no interaction term, no shrinkage, no opponent adjustment beyond the addition itself. It is the quick-look version of what a matchup layer does with more structure, and its failure mode is known: it double-counts when both sides' numbers were built against weak schedules.

**WHICH LAYER.** Matchups — as a presentation format (one number per mismatch, components visible) more than as a model.

The live 2026 board is consistent with the posts' figures (Williams 84.1 at #5 on the board as crawled, vs 84.4 in-post — different weeks of the same season).

**WHICH LAYER.** Matchups (QB/player evaluation input) — a free, *documented* alternative in the PFF-grade class, with the documentation itself being the differentiator: weights philosophy published, era adjustment stated, replacement baseline stated.

# SYNTHESIS

**The pull's center of gravity is not what its roster promised.** A pull aimed at "advanced data and analytics" returned, by volume, mostly fantasy content and fan republication — but its method residue is unusually high-quality, and it clusters into four groups:

1. **Calibration as a publishing act.** cmain7's band-by-band ownership bias table, FantasyPros Labs' expected-vs-actual design, PRFFBall's "expected 3.05, actual 3," jhnhrris publishing an MAE that ties Vegas, SetProb's tier table whose bottom tier sits at 52%, LimitlessSlate posting its −4.5u day. Six independent operators in one week's pull publish their own error measurements. That is the honesty standard GSE already claims; the pull shows the *formats* — each one cheap, each one different, all of them more credible than a record line.
2. **Provenance is the recurring failure.** One stat (aDOT) is six numbers; one matchup split (Young vs the blitz) appears three times with three different values; one platform (StatRankings) runs two models under one name; one metric (Catchable Ball Rate, from the Oct 29 runs) is uncomputable from public data at all. D3 is not an anecdote — it is the week's theme, and the fix is boring: pin every external number to a named source and definition before it enters the engine.
3. **The adjustment layers are where public modeling is differentiating.** MossPicks' five weighted adjustments, Patton's six tendency components, FantasyPros' absence asymmetries, Timo's leverage correction — none of these are new base stats. All of them are *corrections and adjustments applied to base stats*: situational, personnel, coaching, selection-bias. That is precisely GSE's doctrine order (matchup/situation/health adjustments over a stats base, market last), arriving independently from four directions in a single week's pull.
4. **Coach quantification is real now.** Patton's v3.0 is a complete, published, process-only play-caller framework whose construction (personnel entropy, sequencing predictability, PROE+pace) is 5/6 reproducible from public play-by-play. Coach-vs-coach has been a named doctrine layer without a public reference implementation; it has one now.

**Test order (proposed):** (1) Patton approximation — build the 5 public components on nflverse and compare rankings to his published tendencies posts (validates both his model and GSE's personnel/sequencing data plumbing). (2) Definition registry — seed it with the aDOT agreement classes and the three blitz-split variants found here. (3) Paired-flip leverage — adopt as the standing construction before any leverage content is published. (4) Absence-asymmetry correction — fold the FantasyPros findings into the role-shift adjustment as a documented prior until GSE's own absence data can estimate it.

## Deep reproduction — nfl_simulator / Deserve-To-Win (repo dossier) — reports/2026-10-30-NFL-SIMULATOR-DOSSIER.md

**REPRODUCED EXACTLY; the method story is refuted.** From the shipped code (github.com/dgrifka/nfl_simulator, MIT) + nflverse: CAR @ GB deserve-to-win **88%** (p_home 0.8799), likely points **GB 22.3 / CAR 12.7** — exact matches to the post, after a control game (the repo README's CIN @ CLE example) matched to 4 decimals first (0.7488; 16.26 / 11.11). The "40K simulations" figure matches the shipped model's 40,000 draws; the word "simulations" does not — and the method post's claim (every loose ball, field goal and drop re-priced; "160K reruns") **does not describe the shipped model**: shipped v2 never looks at a field goal, extra point, drop, punt or kickoff and re-prices nothing; that was retired v1, which needs paid FTN charting. v2 is a success-rate + yards/play normal model. **Verdict: TEST → adopt for the postgame grading lane only** — never pick formation; the author's own tests say stripping luck does not improve next-game prediction; quote the interval beside the percent. The two posts (method post 2095239309167042695; CAR@GB post 2116043919347638507) are cross-referenced in ON1's catch-up confirmations.

### #1 — @sfdata9ers — Defensive EPA/play allowed by quarter (FOOTBALL — full dossier)

- Post: https://x.com/sfdata9ers/status/2115963896129597592 · CATCH-UP TARGET CLOSED.
- **WHAT IT IS:** a 32-team table of defensive EPA/play allowed split by quarter (Q1/Q2/Q3/Q4/Overall), 2026 Weeks 1–7. Read from the chart: Minnesota is the league's best defense overall (−0.220) and collapses games late (Q4 −0.540); Seattle −0.115, Tampa Bay −0.108, Denver −0.049, Kansas City −0.043, Pittsburgh −0.041 overall; Buffalo is worst (+0.148) and uniformly bad across all four quarters (+0.121/+0.156/+0.149/+0.154). The method is plain nflverse-class EPA aggregated by quarter — the *split* is the contribution: it separates script/pace effects (Q1), halftime-adjustment quality (Q3), and closer strength (Q4) into four numbers per defense.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** @sfdata9ers, powered by @FantasyPtsData per the account bio. The EPA values are CITED from the chart, not reproduced this run — but the construction is fully reproducible from nflverse play-by-play GSE already holds (EPA by posteam/defteam × quarter), and this account's earlier tables were reproduced in-house in the AM repro pass (missed tackles) and ON-CORPUS.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** one group-by on the warehouse pbp (defteam × qtr, EPA mean, Weeks 1–7). No new data source. The Q4 column is the one with prop/grading use: a defense at −0.540 in Q4 is a live-betting and 2H-card fact, and the 1H/2H split is exactly the breakout the 360° card standard already demands.
- **WHICH LAYER:** GSE engine **matchups layer** (defense quality by game phase), feeding the **situations layer** (halftime/2H releases) and the vault's 1H-subset breakout.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** (1) Pair the defensive quarter split with an offensive quarter split (the corpus already holds @sfdata9ers' QB EPA/play by quarter, ON-CORPUS) to build a phase-matrix per matchup — four mini-games instead of one. (2) Buffalo's flat-bad profile vs Minnesota's late-clamp profile are different *kinds* of bad/good: flat profiles price full-game markets, sloped profiles price half markets — the slope itself is a publishable reasoning line.
- **RISKS:** 7-week samples per quarter-cell are ~150–250 plays; Q4 EPA is score-state contaminated (leading defenses face pass-heavy scripts — which cuts both ways and must be stated, not hidden). Chart-read values carry reading error.
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** reproduce the table from nflverse W1–7 and diff against the chart's six named rows. **LEARN-ONLY** — method owned on reproduction; chart digits stay CITED until then.


### #2 — @sfdata9ers — Red Zone Offenses ranked by points per red-zone trip (FOOTBALL — full dossier)

- Post: https://x.com/sfdata9ers/status/2115956346239537416 · CATCH-UP TARGET CLOSED.
- **WHAT IT IS:** all 32 offenses ranked by points scored per red-zone trip (XP and 2-point conversions excluded), Weeks 1–7, with trips, TD%, FG%, and scored%. Read from the chart: SF #1 (22 trips, 86.4% TD%, 100% scored, 5.59 pts/trip), NO #2 (5.18), BUF #3 (5.08), DAL and ATL 5.00; bottom: WAS 3.94, TEN 3.79, and **GB last at 3.46 despite 26 trips (46.2% TD%, only 69.2% scored)** — a volume-rich, conversion-poor profile that was live context for the CAR@GB spotlight the same night. Points-per-trip is the right denominator choice: it prices a trip's full expectation (TD/FG/empty) instead of the TD%-only ranking most charts publish.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** @sfdata9ers / @FantasyPtsData. CITED from the chart; reproducible from pbp (drives ending inside the 20, points from play outcomes excl. XP/2pt).
- **HOW TO USE IT:** buildable in-house from the same pbp pull as #1. As an input it wants a shrinkage note: 16–27 trips per team is a small sample — the honest published form is pts/trip with trip count beside it, exactly as the chart does.
- **WHICH LAYER:** **matchups layer** (finishing quality vs upcoming red-zone defense — pairs directly with #3's SEA note and with @KoalatyStats' red-zone XTD funnels already in the corpus), and the **DFS/packages surface** (TD-scorer props price off exactly this).
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** GB's profile (most trips among the bottom, worst conversion) is a field-goal/kicker-prop shape: trips without TDs are kicker points. A "trips × conversion gap" table flags kicker and team-total-under angles that a TD% ranking alone misses.
- **RISKS:** small samples; red-zone trip definition (snap inside the 20 vs drive reaching the 20) varies by source — pin GSE's definition before comparing across sources (the aDOT lesson from ON-CORPUS D3 applies to every charted stat).
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** reproduce SF/GB endpoints from pbp. **LEARN-ONLY.**


### #3 — @sfdata9ers — Points Allowed vs Yards Allowed scatter (FOOTBALL — full dossier)

- Post: https://x.com/sfdata9ers/status/2115947538666643482 · CATCH-UP TARGET CLOSED.
- **WHAT IT IS:** a per-game scatter, x = yards allowed/game (~240–390), y = points allowed/game (12–30), Weeks 1–7, with the post's own reads: KC and Jacksonville allow plenty of yardage but tighten in the red zone; Seattle ranks 30th in red-zone defense and pays on the scoreboard. Read positions: MIN best (~12.5 pts), SEA fewest yards (~235) but ~19 pts, KC ~17.3 pts on ~335 yds, JAX ~17 pts on ~350 yds, BUF worst (~28.5 pts, ~385 yds), WAS/CAR ~29 pts. The metric pair is a divergence detector: the vertical distance from the yards→points trend line *is* red-zone/turnover/short-field defense, compressed into one picture.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** @sfdata9ers. CITED; reproducible from pbp + drive data in-house.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** the residual (points allowed minus points predicted from yards allowed) is the computable form — one regression on team-game rows GSE already has. Use the residual, not the picture.
- **WHICH LAYER:** **matchups layer** — it is the defensive mirror of #2, and the pair (#2 offense finishing × #3 defense divergence) is a complete red-zone matchup read for any game.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** a team above the line (yards without points — KC/JAX) is a team-total-under / opponent-FG shape; a team below it (SEA) is the opposite. The residual also disciplines the eye: "30th in red-zone defense" is doing the explanatory work in the post, and the residual quantifies how much of SEA's points-allowed is finishing vs yardage.
- **RISKS:** points allowed includes defensive/ST scores and short fields from turnovers — the residual is a bundle, not a pure red-zone measure; 7 games per team.
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** compute the residual table in-house; check KC/JAX positive and SEA negative as the sanity case. **LEARN-ONLY.**


### #4 — @sfdata9ers — QB throwaway rate list (FOOTBALL — full dossier)

- Post: https://x.com/sfdata9ers/status/2115935459167940886 · CATCH-UP TARGET CLOSED.
- **WHAT IT IS:** throwaway rate per QB (throwaways as a share of attempts; min 70 attempts; data @FantasyPtsData), Weeks 1–7. Top: Bryce Young 12.7%, Bo Nix 11.5%, Jayden Daniels 11.2%, Caleb Williams 10.5%, Jalen Hurts 8.4%. Middle read from the chart: Murray 7.2%, Mahomes 6.8%, Darnold 6.8%, Maye 6.5%, Rodgers 6.5%, Allen 6.4%, Ward 6.2%, Jones 5.4%, Penix 4.9%, Stroud 4.9%, Herbert 4.4%, Cousins 4.3%, Brissett 4.3%, Prescott 4.0%, Lawrence 3.8%, Love 3.7%, Goff 3.1%. Bottom: Purdy 2.8%, Mayfield 2.8%, Winston 2.5%, Stafford 2.3%, Burrow 1.9%, Willis 1.3%, Lamar Jackson lowest at 1.0%. (A few mid-list ranks were partially legible in the capture; the endpoints and named values above were legible.) Throwaway rate is a *decision* stat: it prices how a QB resolves a dead play — throw it away, eat a sack, force it, or run.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** charted data (@FantasyPtsData) — throwaways are a charting judgment, not a pbp field; nflverse pbp does not carry a reliable throwaway flag. Values CITED, not reproducible from public pbp — this is the boundary of the in-house repro program, and the dossier says so plainly.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** as a cited input with source pinned (FantasyPtsData definition), in combination: throwaway rate × pressure rate ≈ sack-avoidance profile. Young at 12.7% with GB's pressure night (see #15: 24 pressures, 2.29s time-to-pressure) is the same story told from both sides — he was throwing away because the alternative was sacks, and his −22 net passing yards under pressure is the cost side.
- **WHICH LAYER:** **matchups layer (QB behavior vs pass rush)** — the QB-behavior track that the corpus's two-clock TTT split (#21 PM run) and pocket-state EPA (#16 below) also feed. Direct prop relevance: high-throwaway QBs suppress INT props but also suppress completion volume; low-throwaway QBs (Jackson 1.0%) resolve dead plays by running or forcing — different prop shapes entirely.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** the list inverts a lazy narrative — the top of the list (Young, Nix, Daniels, Williams) is young QBs coached to live for the next down; the bottom is veterans who extend. As content, "who refuses to throw it away, and what it costs/earns" is a clean explainer with a real table behind it.
- **RISKS:** charting-definition variance (what counts as a throwaway vs a spike vs an overthrow is a judgment — cross-source comparisons need the definition registry); min-70-attempts sample includes part-time starters (McKee, Willis) whose rates are small-sample.
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** no in-house repro possible from pbp; file as CITED input, source-pinned. **LEARN-ONLY.**


### #5 — @sfdata9ers — Sack EPA: QB fault or not (FOOTBALL — full dossier)

- Post: https://x.com/sfdata9ers/status/2115916332780933232 · CATCH-UP TARGET CLOSED.
- **WHAT IT IS:** a scatter of team sack damage: x = total sack EPA lost (~9–46), y = the portion of sack EPA charted as the QB's fault (0–18), data charted by @FTNFantasy, Weeks 1–7. Read positions: Tampa Bay highest QB-fault share (~18 of ~34), Pittsburgh ~14.5 of ~43, New Orleans ~13.5 of ~31, NY Giants ~12.5 of ~27; Dallas lowest total damage (~11) with ~9 on the QB; Indianapolis ~6 QB-fault of a large ~42 total (protection/scheme damage); NY Jets ~0 QB-fault of ~40 (pure line failure). The construction splits a team stat into a QB component and a line/scheme component — an attribution method, not just a ranking.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** FTN charting via @sfdata9ers. CITED — fault attribution is human charting; not reproducible from pbp. The *shape* of the analysis (split a loss into actor shares) is the transferable part.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** as a cited matchup input for sack/INT props and for protection reasoning: a QB-fault-heavy team (TB) travels with the QB; a line-fault team (NYJ, IND) is an opponent-matchup variable. GSE cannot compute the split in-house without charting; it can compute total sack EPA lost from pbp and carry the split as a cited overlay.
- **WHICH LAYER:** **matchups layer (pass rush vs QB/protection)**, props lane for sack markets.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** combine with #4: throwaway rate is the QB's *escape valve* for the same pressure that produces QB-fault sacks. A QB high on both (takes QB-fault sacks AND throws away often) is seeing pressure he can't solve; a QB high-fault/low-throwaway is holding the ball by choice. The 2×2 is a QB-under-pressure fingerprint from two cited tables.
- **RISKS:** fault charting is the most judgment-heavy class of stat in the corpus; two charters will split the same sack differently. Small counts (a team's sack total through 7 weeks is 15–35 plays) — shares swing on 2–3 plays.
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** none in-house; CITED overlay only. **LEARN-ONLY.**

### #1 — @wheatonbrando — QB metrics, Weeks 4–8 only: CPOE × EPA/play (FOOTBALL — full dossier)

- Post: https://x.com/wheatonbrando/status/2116039161480110492 (12:27 AM, Oct 30)
- **WHAT IT IS:** a QB scatter for 2026 regular-season Weeks 4–8 only, x = completion percentage over expected (CPOE), y = EPA/play, filters stated on the chart (win probability 0–100%, all downs/quarters, min 20 plays). Read positions: Drake Maye top (~0.45 EPA/play), Joe Burrow ~0.33, Josh Allen and C.J. Stroud ~0.30, Caleb Williams ~0.28. The post's premise is the method: the early weeks now behave like preseason (starters barely play August), so current QB form should be measured from Week 4 forward. Discarding Weeks 1–3 is a *window* decision — the same class of decision as @KoalatyStats' 2-week half-life (ON1 #12), taken from the opposite side: he downweights the recent past's opposite end.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** Brandon Anderson (@wheatonbrando). The chart is a standard nflverse-style build (CPOE + EPA are nflverse fields); values CITED from the chart, fully reproducible in-house from pbp GSE already holds.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** one filtered group-by on the warehouse pbp (Weeks 4–8, QB plays, mean EPA + CPOE). No new data.
- **WHICH LAYER:** **matchups layer (QB form)** — the current-form prior the matchup reasoning starts from, and a candidate replacement for any full-season QB table GSE publishes.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** the corpus now holds three independent recency treatments — drop Weeks 1–3 (this), exponential 2-week half-life (Koalaty), and full-season raw (most charts). GSE can settle which one actually describes its settled history better instead of borrowing any of them on faith: score each window's QB ordering against next-game QB performance in the warehouse. That bake-off is the real find here.
- **RISKS:** the Week-4 cutoff is asserted, not measured, in the post; min-20-plays is a very low bar for a 5-week window (part-time QBs can enter); the 0–100% win-probability filter means garbage time counts, which inflates trailing QBs' EPA.
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** run the three-window bake-off on settled history. **LEARN-ONLY.**


### #2 — @GridironInfo_ — Points allowed off turnovers, through Week 7 (FOOTBALL — full dossier)

- Post: https://x.com/GridironInfo_/status/2115949551760838804 (6:31 PM, Oct 29)
- **WHAT IT IS:** a 32-team bar chart of points a defense has *allowed off turnovers* — points scored by opponents on possessions that began with a takeaway, defensive TDs included (stated on the chart). Fewest: NY Jets 0, Houston 6, Detroit 7, Buffalo/Jacksonville/Kansas City/Miami 10. Most: New Orleans 52, Seattle 47, LA Chargers 47, Tampa Bay ~46. The stat bundles three things: how often your offense hands the ball over in bad spots is *not* in it (this is the defense's side only) — it is short-field defense plus scoop/pick-six leakage, i.e., the part of "points allowed" that is closest to variance.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** @GridironInfo_ (stats/info account). CITED from the chart; the construction is reproducible from pbp + drive data (turnover plays, ensuing drive outcomes, defensive scores) with GSE's own definition pinned first.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** buildable in-house in one pass over the warehouse; publish as a companion column beside raw points-allowed (pairs with ON1 #3's points-vs-yards divergence residual — both are "points allowed, decomposed" views).
- **WHICH LAYER:** **everything-else / situations layer (descriptive variance accounting)** — and the postgame grading lane: it is a third luck-adjacent ledger column next to deserve-to-win (reproduced in-house, dedicated dossier) and net lucky wins.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** NYJ at 0 across 7 weeks is the kind of extreme that is either a real short-field defense skill or the season's luckiest cell — the reasoning value is in saying which evidence would separate the two (opponent starting field position after takeaways is in pbp; the split is computable).
- **RISKS:** 7-week counts are small (a single pick-six swings ~7 points = several ranks); "includes defensive TDs" mixes a rare-event term into a drive-based stat; turnover *locations* (the offense's fault) drive the opportunity set, so the ranking partly grades the team's own offense.
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** reproduce from pbp with a pinned definition; check the NYJ/NO endpoints. **LEARN-ONLY.**

### #1 — @boxscorescout — Chase Brown: top buy-low RB by Expected Fantasy Points (FOOTBALL — full dossier)

- Post: https://x.com/boxscorescout/status/2115912021636161750 (4:01 PM, Oct 29)
- **WHAT IT IS:** A "points over expected" rushing table (data: nflverse, boxscorescout.com): for each qualified RB, expected fantasy points per game (xFP/G — "what an average player scores with the same opportunities") vs actual points per game, lowest difference first. The payload rows: Chase Brown (CIN) is the league's biggest under-performer vs opportunity — 13.5 xFP/G (RB13 opportunity rank) vs 10.1 PTS/G, **−3.3 diff**, actual rank RB23. Behind him: Kendre Miller −3.2, Ashton Jeanty −2.3 (on RB3-level opportunity, 17.3 xFP/G), J.K. Dobbins −2.0, Kaelon Black −1.7, Tyler Allgeier −1.6, MarShawn Lloyd −1.5, Jeremiyah Love −1.5, Woody Marks −1.3, Tony Pollard −1.2. The post's news hook: Brown now faces Tennessee *without Jeffery Simmons*.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** @boxscorescout's own build on nflverse (footer on the chart). Values CITED from the table (10 of 41 qualified shown); the xFP model itself (how opportunity is valued — carries, targets, field position) is the author's, not specified in the post.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** xFP is computable in-house in principle — opportunity shares are nflverse fields — but the author's exact opportunity valuation is his model; GSE can build its own version (rush/target share × situation) and should name it as its own. The immediate use is the *form*: opportunity-minus-output as a regression candidate list.
- **WHICH LAYER:** **usage layer (layer 1 of the weekly order)** — this is a usage-first artifact: it ranks by opportunity before output, exactly the layer order the engine already runs. Secondarily matchups: the Simmons absence is the named-player health fact that turns a regression candidate into a Week 8 case.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** Pair xFP-diff with the corpus's target-funnel tables (Koalaty, reproduced in-house): a player under-performing opportunity *into a funnel defense* is the two-signal version of this post's one-signal claim. And the table's tail matters too — Pollard at −1.2 on RB15 opportunity is the quieter, larger-sample case.
- **RISKS:** 5–7 games per player; "points over expected" inherits half-PPR/scoring settings unstated on the chart; buy-low framing assumes opportunity persists (coaches bench under-performers — the opportunity itself is the risk); the chart shows Tyler Allgeier under ARI (he is an ARI-listed row on the chart as captured — team labels in screenshots carry transcription risk, flagged).
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** build the in-house opportunity-minus-output table from warehouse pbp for RBs and compare its top-5 against this list. **LEARN-ONLY.**

- Post: https://x.com/boxscorescout/status/2115902219136680288 (3:22 PM, Oct 29; 210.5K views — the run's most-engaged post)
- **WHAT IT IS:** A hindsight-optimal 12-team, 10-round snake draft board graded by FPOR/G — fantasy points over replacement per game (half-PPR), replacement defined against the waiver-level player at each position, ADP from Yahoo/Sleeper via FantasyPros, data nflverse. The headline: **10 RBs in round 1** (Gibbs, Walker III, Smith-Njigba the lone early WR, Taylor, McCaffrey, K. Williams, J. Williams, Henry, Hubbard, Lamb, plus two more RBs). The author's own thread concedes the method's soft spot — replacement level is a definition, and an injured player's slot still returns replacement points in his construction.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** @boxscorescout, boxscorescout.com/big-board (linked in thread). Values CITED; smallest-print FPOR/G figures (≈+9.5 down to ≈+6 at the top) not fully legible.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** Not an engine input — a *method* artifact for the DFS/season-long side: FPOR/G is the correct currency for comparing across positions, and GSE's DFS packages make cross-position value claims that should be denominated the same way.
- **WHICH LAYER:** **everything-else / DFS product layer** — and a content asset: "the perfect draft nobody had" is a proven engagement shape (210K views) that GSE's Content OS can run with its own warehouse numbers after each week, labeled hindsight.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** The honest version is the interesting one: re-run the board *using only information available at draft time* (preseason projections as the "pick") and grade the projection systems themselves by FPOR/G — a projection-accuracy ledger, which is a product GSE could sell and nobody in the corpus is building.
- **RISKS:** Hindsight boards are survivorship in a grid — they grade outcomes, not decisions; replacement-level definition drives the RB-heavy result (scarce-position math), so the "10 RBs" headline is partly an artifact of the denominator.
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** none for the engine; file the FPOR/G denomination for DFS package copy. **LEARN-ONLY.**


### #3 — @The_Coach_A — Big Nickel: Graham's 37% run-blitz protects Pittsburgh's light slot defenders (FOOTBALL — full dossier)

- Post: https://x.com/The_Coach_A/status/2116135289852748090 (6:49 AM, Oct 30 — the newest post in this run)
- **WHAT IT IS:** A scheme post (MatchQuarters; full breakdown paywalled at matchquarters.com, linked) on Steelers DC Patrick Graham: as Big Nickel/base usage rises, Pittsburgh's slot defenders are sub-200 pounds, so Graham attacks *early downs* with a **37% run-blitz rate** — interior pressures on Mike "Cross" and Will "Dog" insert paths, paired with Fire Zone (3-under/3-deep) rotations behind them, *instead of* stunting the front. The pressure is a "forced fit": penetration cuts off the zone track while dropping safeties vise the box, guaranteeing a low-yardage down. The blitz is not primarily a pass weapon — it is run-fit insurance for a personnel weakness.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** Cody Alexander (@The_Coach_A), film-based; the 37% figure is his charting, CITED. The graphic ("THE VISE") diagrams the funnel between the hashes vs the Saints.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** The measurable shadow: early-down blitz rate by defense is computable from pbp + blitz charting (FTN-class data); nflverse alone won't carry blitz flags at this fidelity, so in-house reproduction is partial — the *concept* is usable today in reasoning ("this defense run-blitzes to protect light DBs; its early-down pressure numbers are run fits, not pass rush").
- **WHICH LAYER:** **matchups layer (defensive design vs offensive personnel)** — specifically it corrects a misread the engine could make from ON2's pressure tables: a high early-down pressure rate can be a *run* scheme, and grading it as pass-rush strength double-counts it.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** The general principle — *a defense's blitz rate is partly a confession about its personnel* — pairs with #5's QB-side mirror (pressure faced is partly the QB's own creation). Both posts say the same thing from opposite sides: pressure stats are two-party artifacts. A card that cites pressure without an attribution split is citing half a fact.
- **RISKS:** Single-team, single-game film basis (vs Saints) for a season-rate claim; 37% is charted, not reproduced; the full install is behind MatchQuarters' paywall (not pursued).
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** none in-house at blitz fidelity; file as the run-blitz attribution rule beside #5. **LEARN-ONLY.**

Both reps exist in the same game — the post's diagrammed rep has Williams blitzing — but the interim version presented the drop rep as the post's content. The post's text governs; the divergence is recorded here plainly. The game facts stand verified (GB 23, DAL 13; GB's disguised pressure was the game's story at three independent outlets).
- **WHICH LAYER:** **matchups layer (defensive scheme vs QB protection-setting)** — completes the 3-run GB profile: Quarters identity (ON1 #14), pressure production (ON2: 2.29s time-to-pressure), disguise mechanism (here).
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** as filed in the interim version and still valid: pressure has three sources — volume, disguise, one elite rusher — with opposite implications per QB; and "the man Dak accounted for is not the man who came" is a tease-shaped content line (no picks) for the next GB card.
- **RISKS:** Film-mechanism claim, one game; "at volume" for weak rotation is asserted, not counted, in the post.

### #5 — @PattonAnalytics — How well QBs mitigate pressure: POE × pressure-to-sack (FOOTBALL — full dossier)

- Post: https://x.com/PattonAnalytics/status/2115904066555625503 (3:30 PM, Oct 29; StatRankings chart)
- **WHAT IT IS:** A QB scatter separating the two halves of pressure: x = Pressure Over Expectation (POE, −0.15 to +0.10 — how much *more or less* pressure a QB faces than his line/scheme context expects), y = pressure-to-sack conversion (10% best at top to 40% at bottom). Read positions (approximate, from the chart): Prescott best overall (~11% conversion at POE ≈ −0.01 — ordinary pressure faced, almost never converted); Burrow near top; Mahomes ~15%, Stafford ~16%; Purdy ~17% despite facing the *least* pressure relative to expectation (−0.13, tied with Maye ~21%); league reference ≈23% conversion, −0.02 POE; the bad corner: Geno Smith ~41% at −0.145 (little pressure, converts it to sacks anyway), Kyler Murray ~36%; Jones (IND) ~30% at −0.11; the high-pressure survivors: Daniels ~22% at +0.09, Herbert ~29% at +0.08, Mayfield ~27% at +0.10.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** Steven Patton / StatRankings (first-party). POE's expectation model is StatRankings' — inputs unstated on the chart. Values CITED, placements approximate.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** Pressure-to-sack rate is pbp-computable in-house (pressures are the charted input — FTN-class; sacks are pbp). POE is the proprietary half. GSE can build the conversion half today and treat POE as a cited overlay.
- **WHICH LAYER:** **matchups layer (QB vs defensive pressure)** — this is the attribution split #3 demands from the QB side: a defense's sack rate against Geno Smith and against Prescott are not the same achievement, and a QB's sack rate behind a good line (Smith) vs a bad situation (Herbert) are not the same failure.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** Cross with ON1's sack-EPA QB-fault chart (sfdata9ers/FTN): that one splits sack *cost* by fault; this one splits sack *frequency* by cause. Together they are a complete QB-under-pressure fingerprint from two independent sources — exactly the kind of paired artifact that belongs on a 360° card's QB section.
- **RISKS:** POE model opaque; conversion rates on ~half-season pressure counts are noisy (a QB with 60 pressures moves ~1.7 pts per sack); chart placements are visual reads.
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** compute in-house pressure-to-sack by QB from the warehouse's pressure source and compare the extremes (Prescott/Smith) against this chart. **LEARN-ONLY.**

### #1 — @boxscorescout — Defensive play-caller tenures, 1999–2026: Evero second-worst (FOOTBALL — full dossier)

- Post: https://x.com/boxscorescout/status/2116179167016599973 (9:43 AM, Oct 30; thread continuation 2116179480876347769 credits the play-caller data to @SamHoppen)
- **WHAT IT IS:** A ranking of defensive play-caller tenures (minimum 50 games, by team stint, 1999–2026 regular season, 85 tenures total, top 10 shown) by success rate allowed, with EPA/play allowed, points/game, and record alongside. In the visible table, the highest success rate allowed is Arizona under Nick Rallis (47.6%, EPA/play allowed +0.08), followed by Carolina under Ejiro Evero (46.2%, +0.08). The rest of the shown ten are all at 44.9–46.0% success rate allowed, with EPA/play allowed between −0.01 and +0.03. The post's claim, paraphrased: Evero's Carolina tenure is the second-worst 50+ game defensive play-caller tenure since 1999 on both measures.
- **WHERE IT COMES FROM:** @boxscorescout; the chart footer credits nflverse for play data and @SamHoppen for play-caller attribution; the tool home is boxscorescout.com (already verified as the author's site in earlier runs). Values CITED from the chart; not reproduced in-house this run.
- **HOW TO USE IT:** Play-caller attribution is the hard input — a season-by-season, team-by-team caller table joined to nflverse play-by-play. With that join, EPA/play and success rate allowed per tenure are plain aggregations GSE's warehouse can run. Without the attribution table, the chart is a cited reference only.
- **WHICH LAYER:** **Matchups layer** — coordinator-vs-coordinator is an explicit matchup input in Garrett's doctrine, and this is the first corpus artifact that grades the defensive caller as a multi-year tenure rather than a single-season team defense. Secondarily the situations layer for Carolina opponents while Evero remains the caller.
- **CREATIVE ANGLES:** Pair a caller's tenure grade with his current roster's personnel tier (ON3's personnel trilogy): a bottom-graded caller with bottom-tier personnel is a different bet than the same caller with a real roster. The 85-tenure table is also a ready-made "coach effect" prior: how much of a defense's EPA is the caller, how much is the roster — a variance decomposition GSE could publish as reasoning.
- **RISKS:** Tenure grades confound caller, roster, era, and schedule; 50-game minimum selects for coaches who kept jobs despite results (survivorship in reverse); success-rate and EPA definitions are nflverse-standard but the exact play filters are the author's.
- **FIRST TEST / VERDICT:** Build the caller-attribution join for 2023–2026 only and reproduce Evero's Carolina line; if it lands within rounding of the chart, extend back. **TEST.**


### #2 — @The_Coach_A — Vikings double-mug "pick" pressure vs combo protection (FOOTBALL — full dossier)

- Post: https://x.com/The_Coach_A/status/2116168242947649998 (9:00 AM, Oct 30; full breakdown on MatchQuarters, linked in post; 14-second film clip attached)
- **WHAT IT IS:** A scheme mechanism, paraphrased from the post: in double-mug alignments (both inside linebackers walked up on the line), centers and running backs typically work together to pick up both mugged linebackers. Minnesota's variation converts the usual off-ball cross-dog (linebackers crossing through opposite gaps) into a "pick" pressure designed to defeat exactly that combo block and stress the offense's weakest protection link. The post text truncates at the tail in X's rendering; the mechanism above is the legible portion.

- **HOW TO USE IT:** Film-level mechanism, not a computable stat from nflverse alone. Its use is interpretive: when Minnesota's pressure rate spikes against a team whose center/RB combo is its protection plan, this is the named reason to expect it.
- **WHICH LAYER:** **Matchups layer (defensive scheme vs protection scheme)** — completes a Minnesota pressure trilogy in the corpus with the Flores run-fit and boundary-overload posts from earlier runs, now with the pass-protection counterpart.

## EXTRA100 final sweep (100 posts) — reports/2026-10-30-EXTRA100.md

**NGS provenance reconciliation (the run's most valuable single item, carried in full):** @NextGenStats RT @MinaKimes (2116230019991388579) — Green Bay pressured Bryce Young on **47%** of dropbacks in the Carolina game per NGS; the **52%** figure circulating was from the Tampa game the prior week. SumerSports charting separately puts GB's CAR-game pressure rate at 52.2% (93rd percentile). Three numbers, three provenances — the corpus now keeps them separate instead of conflated.


### A1. Pressure-rate vs blitz-rate gap decomposition — @PocketContext (2116263789272432641) — LEARN-ONLY ★

- **What it is:** For each 2026 QB (33 charted, 29 with ≥150 dropbacks), plot pressure rate faced against blitz rate faced (Next Gen Stats) and read the **gap** between them. Pressure exceeds blitz most for Justin Herbert (+15.9 pts), Geno Smith (+12.1), Bryce Young (+11.8) — QBs getting pressured without blitzes, i.e. losing to 4-man rush/coverage. Blitz exceeds pressure for Michael Penix Jr. (+15.2), Caleb Williams (+13.9), Bo Nix (+2.9) — QBs beating the blitz or escaping it.
- **Construction (as-posted, author-stated):** rate gap = pressure% − blitz% per QB, season to date. The author states the bounding logic explicitly: the gap does **not** yield a true non-blitz pressure rate (some blitzes also produce pressures), but it bounds and ranks where pressure is coming from structurally. Author concedes the limit in-post — a rare, honest construction note.
- **Primary source:** NGS pressure/blitz splits. GSE computes this today from nflverse + NGS feeds it already pulls; no new data needed.
- **Engine layer:** matchups (OL vs front, QB vs pressure structure) — feeds directly into the Flores/pressure work already in the corpus (S108 family).
- **Companion post (2116178423458734457):** Herbert vs Love worked example — Herbert 42.1% pressure rate / 26.2% blitz faced (93/221 pressures, 21 sacks, 2.81s time to throw); Love 37.5% / 35.7% (123/328, 14 sacks, 2.58s). Same construction, two QBs, full counting stats in text.
- **Creative angle:** gap sign flips the coaching question — positive gap = fix protection/answers vs 4-man rush; negative gap = the QB is the pressure answer, blitz him less. Pre-game: rank the week's QBs by gap to find which defenses must blitz to get home (and are therefore exposed deep).
- **Risk:** NGS pressure attribution is model-based; single-season sample to Week 8; as-posted values unverified until reproduced.
- **Verdict:** LEARN-ONLY, **register-worthy**.


### A2. Defensive Stuff Rate top-10, values in text — @PattonAnalytics via @StatRankings (2116258849829363769) — LEARN-ONLY

Stuff rate = share of opponent rush attempts stopped at or behind the line. Full table carried in TEXT (unusual for this route): Bengals 23.1% (#1), Steelers 21.7, Browns 21.1, Bills 20.8, Seahawks 20.6, Packers 20.0, Ravens 19.8, Buccaneers 19.4, Vikings 19.3, Falcons 18.7. Construction: StatRankings' defensive stuff rate, season to date; denominator = opponent designed rushes (exact filter as-published by StatRankings, not restated in-post). Engine layer: matchups (run defense vs run offense). Pairs with the corpus's StatRankings work (S89). Values as-posted, unverified.


### A3. Two-point conversion decision study with the query spec in-post — @michaelchamp (2116145878549381197) — LEARN-ONLY

The author publishes the exact nflverse query: teams down 14 that went for 2 after the first touchdown and then scored two touchdowns before the opponent scored again. Worked: 2023 GB–NO, 2023 TEN–MIA, 2025 NYJ–CIN, 2021 LAC–CLE. Failed: 2025 CLE–TEN, 2024 NYG–WAS. Small-n by construction (the filter is the famous "down-14-early" branch of the go-for-2 debate), but the value is the **reproducible spec**: the query is stated precisely enough to re-run and extend in-house (all down-14 first-TD decisions, not only the double-score branch). Engine layer: situations (in-game decision rules). As-posted, unverified.


### A4. Officiating forecast with published receipts — @OpenOfficiating (2115873816836460771) — LEARN-ONLY

Forecast made pre-game: **14.65 accepted flags, 80% range 9–20**. Actual: **13 accepted** (DAL 8 for 47 yds, PHI 5 for 45), 1 declined, 14 thrown — inside the range, and the author states every live flag count in the thread matched. Source: nflverse, checked against ESPN. This is the refs layer (weekly cycle step 5) done the Hermes-pattern way: a public forecast, an interval, a post-game check, a stated hit. Rare in this corpus — most officiating content is complaint, not calibration. As-posted, unverified.


### A5. Luck dashboard thru Week 7 — @DataWithBliss (2115120913632899328) — LEARN-ONLY

Win-probability-swing accounting of the season's most impactful "luck" plays: GB dropped lead-changing TD pass with 3:30 left in Q4 (+36.3% WP for DET), ARI dropped lead-changing TD pass (+25.7% for DEN), IND missed game-tying 48-yd FG with 4:27 left in Q4 (+20.5% for MIN). Provenance matters: DataWithBliss is the upstream source of the luck data behind the run_the_sims Luck+Penalties construction already registered (S107) — this post is that supply chain, visible. Engine layer: everything else (grading/regression context — luck accounting grades results, it never forms plays). Values as-posted, unverified.


### A6. Huddle geometry from tracking data — @DataWithBliss (2115087826832576878) — LEARN-ONLY

Using player tracking data: the median position of each player in the huddle for each team's most common offensive lineup. Novel tracking surface — huddle geometry as a formation/personnel tell (who stands where before the break leaks grouping and possibly play family). No published GSE analog; research direction only. Construction as-posted; the chart itself is image-carried (values gap flagged). Engine layer: everything else / matchup research backlog.


### A7. nflverse success-rate provenance caution — @cgawilson (2115940845157273966) — LEARN-ONLY

"If you're using NFLVerse data, their success rate is still based on EPA. Try PFR." One line, real consequence: nflverse's `success` flag is EPA>0-derived, not the standard down-and-distance definition (1st down: ≥40% of yards to gain; 2nd: ≥60%; 3rd/4th: conversion). Any in-house reproduction that mixes nflverse success with PFR-style success is silently comparing two metrics. Directly relevant to the signal-pack reproduction standards. As-posted claim about a data dictionary — checkable in the nflverse docs, flagged here as the kind of provenance note the corpus keeps.

**F. Repos, tools & agents**
### F1. Hermes Tuning Masterclass — repo VERIFIED (2116216283972747359, part 3; 2116228907297022319, part 1) — TEST ★

1. **What it is:** A six-volume-plus-bonus study/build repo for Nous Research's Hermes Agent — Tony Simons' twelve-part series indexed and illustrated, plus a ten-build track of copy-paste prompts "checked against the official Hermes docs," and a Tuning volume (Vol. 6) that measures what a Hermes install sends before you type and cuts it in nine stages.
2. **Primary source:** github.com/jasonjeske/hermes-master-class — **fetched and verified this run** (page text): public, **7 stars, 1 watcher, 0 forks, 7 commits**, created 2026-09-18, current commit 93d7bd902993c1c5798e59aceb7e80f6e437de20.
3. **Tree/readme:** Root: masterclass/, bots/, company/, desktop/, kits/, skills/hermes-tune/, src/, tips/, tools/, tune/, ATTRIBUTION.md, LICENSE + LICENSE-CODE. Volumes cover the agent, Desktop, Bots (six-bot team: atlas, forge, scout, quill, sentinel, ops — SOUL.md per bot, model pins, routines, shared memory/board), Company, Expert Tips (/steer, /queue, kanban-over-chat), Tuning, and a bonus ranking all 119 slash commands.
4. **License:** listed as "Other (NOASSERTION)" — LICENSE and LICENSE-CODE files exist but the license is not a standard SPDX grant; treat content as read-and-learn, not copy-and-ship, until the license files are read directly.
5. **Activity:** 7 commits since Sept 18 — a finished reference, not a living project.
6. **Fleet fit:** Direct. Garrett runs a Hermes agent; Vol. 6's measurements were taken on a sealed install of Hermes Agent v0.22.5 (per README) — cache warmth, cheap side tasks, runaway caps — and the repo ships a `skills/hermes-tune` skill that audits an install weekly. The part-3 post's own summary ("keep the cache warm and the side tasks cheap, cap the runaways, and audit the install every week") is the tuning doctrine in one line.
7. **Verdict: TEST** — read Vol. 6 against the fleet's actual Hermes install before adopting any setting; the repo's claims are version-pinned (v0.22.5 / v0.21.7), so the first test is version match. Register-worthy.


### F2. Kanzo — agent kanban + MCP server (2116226376437288987, @AverageAiBro) — TEST ★

1. **What it is:** A kanban board in the browser and an MCP server in one small program — humans and coding agents work from the same task list. "Tell your agent to take the next task from kanzo and do it, and it moves the card to doing and comments as it works."
2. **Primary source:** by Emanuele Micheletti (emanuele-em on GitHub), named in-post; repo URL not printed in the captured text (t.co links unexpanded) — **repo page not fetched; stars/activity unverified** (gap flagged).
3. **Construction as-posted:** the project is resolved from the git remote (the board knows which repo a task belongs to); a Backlog column holds ideas agents leave alone until a human promotes them; the board syncs across machines through a **private git repo you own — no account, no server**.
4. **License:** AGPL, as-posted.
5. **Platforms:** macOS and Linux, as-posted.
6. **Fleet fit:** This is the orchestration-board problem (Motif's board, the fleet MCP bus) solved with git as the sync layer instead of a hosted service — directly comparable to the fleet's own MCP bus design, and the Backlog-promotion rule matches Garrett's human-gate doctrine.
7. **Verdict: TEST** — pending repo verification (URL, stars, last commit) before any hands-on. Register-worthy.
